sample_q_texts: For Mendelian inheritance to be transmitted from parent to offspring, it must be expressible in the parental germ cells, which must be passed to the next generation via parents to offspring. However, this traditional Mendelian rule was to a significant extent broken by the occurrence of heterozygous gametes in meiosis I, unlike meiosis II. With the advent of algorithmic approaches to analyze genetic signals, researchers are attempting to "re-write" the rules of Mendelian genetics and reveal the role of sex chromosomes in inheritance. However, the extent to which individual inheritance rules can be modified by sex chromosome mutations is not fully understood. Our work is relevant to human studies of Mendelian inheritance because we used genetic numerical cutoffs to define heterozygous gametes. We utilized the human Intergenic Genetic Diversification (IGVD) dataset in relation to the adult female ovary for germline genomewide (GW) sequencing and pedigree analysis with scATAC-Seq data for analysis of germline gamete expression. We observed significant effects of the sex chromosome on the number of heterozygous gametes for the autosomal dominant STT-2 (SRY)-cDNA region analysis. The STY gene region for the autosomal recessive MP-1 region analysis showed some statistically significant effects of sex chromosomes for the heterozygosity ratio. This raises an important question: if male germ cells are able to make sperm, can female germ cells only make eggs? Or are there other complex behaviors of gametes in Mendelians framework? Some open questions in this area are: are there sexual dimorphisms in intermediate gametes (morphologically-, functionally-, and functionally-derived gametes) besides the oocytes or spermatozoa, and do certain gametes maintain the entire genome of the Zygote (fertilized egg), which has been suggested to only produce oocytes? Moreover, does human inheritance result in the transmission of Mendelian inheritance rules? These questions will require more research to confirm or refute.

Animals harness diverse metabolic resources to produce sex hormones. Yet, the plasma glucose level limits the proliferation and differentiation of rodent and avian oocytes to the production of sex hormones. The dopamine receptor (D2R)-type G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) CRB5, which is localized on the proximal endoplasmic reticulum, regulates oocyte response to dopamine/D2R stimulation. Our previous work showed that local dopamine activation of D2R is essential for mouse oocyte hormone production and elucidates the effects of D2R activation on CRB5. Here, we further identified the CRB5 ligand susceptibility and specificity of CRB5 and used animal models to verify that CRB5 mediates local dopamine activation of D2R-type G proteins and suppresses D2R signaling through the conformational change of CRB5 leading to the expression of oocyte-specific oocyte transcriptional factor to maintain the oocyte proliferation. Our study provides insights into the mechanisms of male hormone production and oocyte functioning and describes the potential pathophysiological implications of local dopamine activation of D2R.

Meiotic non-disjunction anomalies are important etiologic factors of embryonic and fetal loss in reproductive organs. In a cohort of pediatric patients with balanced X-INN-SYMMETRY (XBINS) syndrome, we have investigated the molecular basis of non-disjunction as part of a global research to understand the role of this process during gametogenesis. Since zebrafish display a typical human life cycle, we have developed a model that allows for genetic elucidation and has allowed for in vivo comparison with human in a developmental path.

Terrestrial vertebrates reproduce sexually by constructing and giving birth to fully developed young. Yet the particular cellular and morphological features that give rise to reproductive life are likely to have been shaped by the late evolution of sex. Despite this, sexual reproduction remains largely invariant across vertebrates, and so although many of the stem cells and cell systems that drive lineage divergence are present across vertebrates there is no example of a lineage producing mature life but maintaining the reproductive molecular machinery and cell systems that enables the construction of fully developed young. Here we identify a homolog of the bovine testicle tissue within the zebra finch testes, a highly sexually dimorphic species, and show that this homolog can still produce germ cells during ageing. Transcriptomic studies suggest that the presence of this gene is essential for testis function and organ development, and its conserved genomic and transcriptomic character allows it to be used as a versatile experimental system to investigate the male senescence process and understand the ageing dynamics of the reproductive system in developing tissues.

Hairless hair coat mice provide an ideal resource for the study of human drug metabolism. Here, we describe a large-scale molecular-genetic genome-wide association study of the phenotype 117 loci on the short arm of the mouse X chromosome (XSHC-117) using 1,426 mice with a hair coat phenotype as well as a control population. Two separate screening approaches generated a genotype for 1,391 nonredundant loci, associated with coat color, coat pattern, and coat marking. The most deleterious loci on the XSHC-117 strongly impaired coat patterns. Notably, loss-of-function alleles of genes encoding the collagen: soil peptide matrix (CTS) enzyme and the colonic receptor (CGS) for the mucin MUC2 led to a 5-fold increase in coat color change scores at three loci on XSHC-117. Genetic and biochemical screens revealed that these genes are required for MUC-4 modification and MUC-2 expression in the epithelium. Taken together, our data suggests that the genetic landscape on the X chromosome may be a useful resource for identifying human genes tied to disease phenotypes, including a role for the XSHC-117 in body coat expression.

The historical and ongoing reduction in tail length in the mouse has been attributed to changes in reproductive physiology rather than structural rearrangements. Yet mice still have the opportunity to examine these changes over generations. The effects of natural selection on the tail length as quantified by 138/138 tail length data points for the mouse's T2A-UAS-loxP background strain are analyzed. The G script discovers context-dependent mutation outcomes with variable selection. The G script controls underpopulation extinction with negative selection. Unlike previous analysis methods, this method explicitly controls for overlap, not controlling for it neutralizes the removal of a tail length mutant. The T2A-Gautz effect is detected with this method. Underpopulation events are generally the selected mutations. Even though the analysis did not control for underpopulation events, underpopulation mutations generally still occur in body organs. In conclusion, the analysis methods control for underpopulation death and point out how genome-wide mutation results can be predicted under selective conditions.

In mammalian germ cell development, one mature cell yields two gametes or ova (ovocytes) and the remaining cell is identified as the primary germline stem cell. Organising this cell following the early egg development requires intricate interactions among its epigenetic and transcriptional regulators, and their roles in regulating maturation of germline cells have largely been overlooked. In this study, we utilised two specialised genetic models of the budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Saccharomyces paradoxus, to identify marked sequences within the nascent ovocyte in S. cerevisiae, and specifically between the origins of duplicated genes, which are important for specifying germline cells in S. cerevisiae. We demonstrated that ectopic phosphorylation of the starting sites of these duplicated genes in S. cerevisiae caused aberrant germline development. Transcriptomic analysis revealed a shift of conserved germline genes from the egg to the pupa at the late stage of egg formation, emphasising how co-occurrence of various regulatory elements dictate early development. Based on this finding, we infer that post-translational modifications of the nascent egg contribute to germline differentiation by acting on its epigenome.

Successful animal survival and reproduction depend on the careful balance between production of offspring and metabolic energy reserves used in development, maintenance, and reproduction. Energy strategies within gestations, in particular the timing of breeding, are often shaped by energy requirements, which can be viewed as welfare indicators. Here, we explored the extent to which maternal energy reserves at different ages predict birth weight. This relationship was variable across individuals, traits, and ages. In particular, our results suggest that when females in different demographic stages (i.e., single versus multiple gestations) produced infants with similar birth weights, they had very similar levels of energy reserves at birth.

We also examined how female reproductive age and fecundity were associated with birth weight and energy reserve levels. Older females were associated with lower birth weights and lower energy reserves, while higher fecundity and earlier (versus later) breeding were not significantly associated with lower birth weights or lower energy reserves at birth. To further explore this effect, we examined whether fetal cell mass (FCM) at birth could explain the relationship between maternal age and birth weight. Results indicated that FCM was not a significant predictor of maternal age or birth weight at later ages. In sum, our results suggested that fetal energy reserves do not explain the relationship between maternal age and birth weight in mice.

Significance statementO_LIUnderstanding energy states within gestations is critical for predicting pregnancy failure in humans and non-human mammals, such as mice.
C_LIO_LIWe show that offspring mass at birth and energy reserves at birth independently predict birth weight in non-human mammals, but only offspring mass at birth strongly predicts birth weight in humans.
C_LIO_LIOur findings suggest that energy store levels at birth are not the primary driver of body size, female reproductive age, or breeding phenology in mice.
C_LIO_LIOur research is valuable because it disentangles the unique maternal age-to-birth-weight relationships in mice and underscores the relevance of energy stores to understand not only long-term species fitness but also short-term pregnancy and birth outcomes.
C_LI

Bias and confounding in the preparation of public-use repositories, such as the public mouse phenotype database (pmdb) and drug response (dp) repository, can lead to results being based on invalid assumptions. We examined the effect of false discovery in the analysis of RNA-seq phenotypes on the accuracy of these three repositories. When also including data from the deworming (dipmLD) repository, this assessment showed all repositories suffer from bias in the processing of publicly available experiments. Population statistics were also influenced by this bias, leading to erroneous comparisons between groups or, for example, between cohorts. These examples are highlighted through simulation to illustrate that the subpopulation bias generated by losing or adding experimental designs can lead to variance in population statistics, which in turn impacts on parameter inference. The introduced bias can be eliminated by applying experimental design criteria, for example, complete block designs. This leads to a change in the form of the estimating variance and the standard error of the population parameter. Analyses should therefore be reviewed in light of known estimates of sample size and experimental design, such as the technical design criteria of the dp repository.

Maternal and offspring weight gain throughout pregnancy are important risk factors for childhood obesity. We investigated the relationship between paternal and gestational weight gain during pregnancy and offspring size from 10 to 60 months. Maternal body mass index and maternal (but not paternal) diet and energy intake were measured during pregnancy and to offsprings 6 to 65 months of age. Thirty f344-lbF/F and six New Zealand White F0-males were raised from 9 to 65 months of age, at which time weights were measured along with the expressed degree of leg somites enlargement. No significant differences were noted in maternal body mass index or maternal (but not paternal) energy intake, diet energy intake, or mean body weight between the three groups of gestating mothers. Mothers with larger body mass indexes showed larger body weights and body fat (e.g., increase in tibia length), while those with greater mean body weight tended to have a greater number of leg somites. Overall, mothers with larger total body weight and those with greater mean body weight showed offspring with greater trunk and leg lengths (but no significant difference in leg somites). Each individual somite was enlarged to some degree between these groups, and no significant differences were noted in somite size, tibial bone thickness, or tibial length. These results indicate that individual somites underwent random partitioning, with both sperm and ovum initiating somite number formation, resulting in somite size throughout gestation. Somitic lengthening persisted through offspring development, with male offsprings exhibiting significantly greater somite lengths.
sample_p_texts: Genetic compensation is a common phenomenon in zebrafish in response to genetic alterations. As such, differences between morphant and mutant zebrafish models of human diseases have led to significant difficulties in phenotypic interpretation and translatability. One form of compensation is the maternal deposit of mRNAs and proteins into the oocyte that supports developmental processes before zygotic genome activation. In this study, we generated a zebrafish model of severe congenital muscular dystrophy by targeting protein O-mannose N-Acetylglucosaminyltransferase 2 (pomgnt2), a maternally provided gene that maintains cell-extracellular matrix interactions through glycosylation. Zygotic knockouts (ZKOs) retain protein function in the first week post-fertilization and survive to adulthood, though they develop muscle disease later in life. In contrast, maternal-zygotic KOs (MZKOs) generated from ZKO females develop early-onset muscle disease, reduced motor function, neuronal axon guidance deficits, and retinal synapse disruptions, recapitulating features of the human presentation. While assessing transcriptional changes linked to disease progression, the availability of embryos obtained from different breeding strategies also allowed for direct comparison of ZKOs and MZKOs to define the impact of having a KO mother. We found that offspring from a ZKO mother, independently of genotype, show distinct expression patterns from animals obtained from heterozygous breeding. Some of these changes reflect an increased metabolic requirement, possibly stemming from maternal metabolic disruption. These findings will not only be applicable to other CMD models targeting maternally provided genes but also provide new insight into modeling disease using maternal-zygotic mutants.

The miR-200a and miR-200b families control mouse ovulation and are essential for female fertility. The ZEB1 transcription factor is a conserved target of both families and has been implicated as a key player in female fertility at multiple levels. Using gene-edited mice that express a miR-200a/b-resistant form of Zeb1, we found that derepression of Zeb1 in the female pituitary caused decreased production of luteinizing hormone and anovulatory infertility. These phenotypes were accompanied by widespread changes in pituitary gene expression characterized by decreased levels of ZEB1 targets, which include the miR-200a/b miRNAs, as expected from the miR-200a/b-ZEB1 double-negative feedback loop. Also observed were increased levels of mesenchymal genes, neuronal genes, and miR-200a/b targets. These results show that a double-negative feedback loop centered on the miRNA regulation of a single transcription factor can significantly influence the expression of thousands of genes and have dramatic phenotypic consequences.

Hybrid incompatibility can lead to lethality and sterility of F1 hybrids, contributing to speciation. Here we found that female hybrids between Mus musculus domesticus and Mus spicilegus mice are sterile due to the failure of homologous chromosome separation in oocyte meiosis I, producing aneuploid eggs. This non-separation phenotype was driven by the mis- localization of the cohesin protector, SGO2, along the chromosome arms instead of its typical centromeric enrichment, resulting in cohesin over-protection. The upstream kinase, BUB1, showed a significantly higher activity in hybrid oocytes, explaining SGO2 mis-targeting along the chromosome arm. Higher BUB1 activity was not observed in mitosis, consistent with viable hybrid mice. Cohesion defects were also evident in hybrid mice from another genus, Peromyscus, wherein cohesin protection is weakened. Defective cohesion in oocytes is a leading cause of reduced fertility especially with advanced maternal age. Our work provides evidence that a major cause of human infertility may play a positive role in promoting mammalian speciation.

Mus Musculus has provided scientists a well-adapted animal model for the developmental studies. There is one on one co-relation between molecular determinants such as genes between humans and mice hence making them superior model to study gene expression and to do translation research. Swiss albino mice strain of house mice was used in this study with comparisons of efficiency of pregnancies during two different strategies of mating; i.e., more traditional random/blind mating and more recent timed mating in experimental paradigms to get staged mice embryos. The workflow required for the blind mating was less labor intensive and required minimal maintenance both time and human resource and was easy to execute. On the other hand, timed mating strategy was ideal for getting staged embryos that was efficient in giving pregnancies and was ideal for less equipped labs but however required more maintenance and human resource. The results of comparisons of weight gain with pregnancies was similar in two groups where some un-pregnant mice also showed average or above average weight gain with time. The z-test analysis for difference between two proportions was employed to calculate efficiency of pregnancies in the two groups and p value was found to be 0.06 which suggested that was no significant difference between the two groups however, this might be due to small sample size that was possible in our small setting. The accurate embryonic staging was required in the experiments corresponding to the peak of neurogenesis in mice and embryos were fixed and sectioned and later studied with immunohistochemistry. The timed matings showed to be superior regarding total pregnancies and having accurate stages and is recommended in labs even if in smaller settings and prevent less animal sacrifice.

We examined the effects of X-ray irradiation on Xenopus laevis, focusing on pre- and post-fertilization exposure. We applied X-ray doses of 10, 50, 100, 250, and 500 Gy. Fifty percent of the 360 eggs irradiated at 250 Gy failed to fertilize, while fertilized eggs developed normally until the gastrula stage. Doses ranging from 10 to 250 Gy caused developmental anomalies. High mortality rates were observed at doses of 100 to 500 Gy. Post-fertilization irradiation at 50 to 100 Gy resulted in 100% lethality, while exposure to 10 Gy led to only 13% lethality, although both exposure levels produced similar types of developmental anomalies compared to pre-fertilization irradiation. This study highlights how the timing and intensity of exposure critically affect embryo viability, especially during the sensitive stages of fertilization and gastrulation. We establish the necessary and sufficient dosage to further investigate the molecular mechanisms of X-ray damage to DNA and protein.

HighlightHigh doses of electromagnetic radiation pre- and post-fertilization produce different developmental outcomes in Xenopus laevis.

Nlrp5 encodes a core component of the subcortical maternal complex (SCMC) a cytoplasmic protein structure unique to the mammalian oocyte and cleavage-stage embryo. NLRP5 mutations have been identified in patients presenting with early embryo arrest, recurrent molar pregnancies and imprinting disorders. Correct patterning of DNA methylation over imprinted domains during oogenesis is necessary for faithful imprinting of genes. It was previously shown that oocytes with mutation in the human SCMC gene KHDC3L had globally impaired methylation, indicating that integrity of the SCMC is essential for correct establishment of DNA methylation at imprinted regions. Here, we present a multi-omic analysis of an Nlrp5- null mouse model, which in GV oocytes displays a misregulation of a broad range of maternal proteins, including proteins involved in several key developmental processes. This misregulation likely underlies impaired oocyte developmental competence. Amongst impacted proteins are several epigenetic modifiers, including a substantial reduction in DNMT3L; we show that de novo DNA methylation is attenuated in Nlrp5-null oocytes. This provides evidence for mechanisms leading to downstream misregulation of imprinted genes, which in turn, may result in imprinting syndromes, multi-locus imprinting disturbances (MLID) and hydatidiform moles.

Primordial germ cells (PGCs) are the precursors of the germline and among the first cells to be specified during embryogenesis. Contrary to the common assumption that PGCs directly develop into germline stem cells (GSCs), recent mammalian data and our zebrafish observations suggest a more complex picture. We hypothesized that individual PGCs contribute differentially to gonad development. To test this hypothesis, we developed two Cre-based lineage tracing systems and demonstrate that PGCs give rise to at least four distinct clone types in zebrafish. We observed no restriction in clone type localization along the anterior-posterior axis, suggesting these differences are PGC intrinsic or locally determined. Further examination of the ovarian reserve revealed functional evidence that some PGCs generate self-renewing GSCs, while others produce non-renewing progenitors that are depleted with successive matings. Collectively, our findings propose a revised model of vertebrate germline establishment with implications to reproductive lifespan. This model suggests that differentiation potential varies among PGCs, allowing individual PGCs to directly differentiate into multiple distinct germ cell types, including renewing GSCs and transient populations that contribute to an early wave of gametes.

Fertilization requires the successful binding and fusion of sperm and egg. In zebrafish, sperm-egg binding is mediated by the Spaca6-Izumo1-Tmem81 complex on sperm interacting with Bouncer on the egg. We previously found that expressing medaka Bouncer on zebrafish eggs and vice versa allows hybridization between medaka and zebrafish, two species that can normally not hybridize. Here, we tested whether providing zebrafish Spaca6 and Izumo1 on medaka sperm and vice versa enables cross-species compatibility from the side of the sperm. To this end, we generated spaca6 and izumo1 knock-out (KO) lines in medaka, which are male sterile, and introduced zebrafish spaca6 and izumo1 transgenes. Transgenic medaka males did not fertilize zebrafish or medaka eggs with zebrafish Bouncer. Similarly, zebrafish males expressing medaka Spaca6 and Izumo1 failed to fertilize zebrafish eggs presenting medaka Bouncer. Unexpectedly, providing either full-length medaka Spaca6 or the Bouncer binding site of medaka Izumo1 in zebrafish sperm rescued the sterility of spaca6 and izumo1 KO, respectively. Therefore, medaka Spaca6 and Izumo1 can interact with zebrafish Bouncer when paired with their zebrafish sperm complex members underscoring the nuanced interplay between molecular restrictions and compatibilities during sperm-egg interaction across teleosts.

sample_q_texts: Approximately 80% of ARVD types I and II cases develop certain chronic conditions that can ultimately be fatal. Although most molecular genetic reports have suggested that mitochondria-based (mitochondrial biogenesis defects) ARVD types I and II cause the most severe chronic conditions, how genetic mutations affect mitochondrial function and function of tissues with mitochondrial cristae, such as heart muscle and liver, remains poorly understood. Studying the role of the voltage-gated calcium (CaV) family potassium channels in C-type inter-endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress was used to discover functional mutations that potentially impaired cardiac and liver mitochondria function. The identification of potassium channels with distinct CaV member 1 (CaMV1) and CaMV2 subtype (CaMV3) that showed different gating mechanisms triggered by membrane depolarization. Myocardium cells isolated from neonatal mice showed decreased mitochondrial ATP production, while hepatoma cells from cristae-ablation Drosophila melanogaster had increased ATP-driven mitochondrial electron transport in response to membrane depolarization and loss of mitochondrial cristae. Bioinformatics analysis revealed that mitochondrial CaMV2 channel was overexpressed while mitochondrial CaMV1 channels were poorly expressed, thus altering the available CaV2.1 subunits, which are essential for the smooth functioning of K+ channels in the heart, liver, and skin. Computational genetic analysis of the mutation suggested that the missense amino acid mutations on the transmembrane region could lead to a hydrophobic patch that increased the negative charge on the critical N-terminal extracellular domain, which in turn degraded K+ channels. We demonstrated that the channel activity is altered by uncoupling at a single binding site. Theoretical calculations further support the proposed mechanism for the impact of the mutation on mitochondrial function. This finding indicates the potential role of mutant voltage-sensitive K+ channels in cardiomyopathy.

Mitochondria were shown to be the major source of oxygen radicals that induce cell death in skin keratinocytes, suggesting them to be central to the carcinogenic process. The exact mechanisms underlying this effect have remained elusive. Using cryogenic electron tomography, we explore how the mitochondrial outer membrane enables the generation of reactive oxygen species in human skin keratinocytes. Our observations show that lipid bilayers of the mitochondrial membrane surround the inner membrane infolding, amplifying the permeation of calcium and oxygen into the mitochondrial matrix. Simultaneously, the cholesterol layer at the inner face ensures a consistent lipid retention which enables the production of reactive oxygen species upon lipid peroxidation. Surprisingly, the mitochondrial cytb protein itself is defective, being located in the 1:1 interaction between the inner membrane and the outer membrane, increasing the risk for these hydrogen peroxide generation. In addition, the overexpression of cytochrome c oxidase via transmembrane domains led to the formation of disulfide bonds resulting in a highly reduced membrane. Surprisingly, the charge under non-physiological conditions makes it prone to redox-sensitive conformational changes resulting in membrane damage.

Redox balance is an essential component of life on Earth and the capacity of cells to maintain redox balance has been exploited to develop anticancer and anti-inflammatory agents that target redox mechanisms. The glycolytic enzyme Complex I of the antioxidant enzyme system can dissociate into dozens of different sub-complexes that are dependent on glucose dehydrogenase (GDH), pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH), triose phosphate isomerase (TPI), aldehyde dehydrogenase 1 (ALDH1) or dehydrogenases. The separation of glycolytic enzymes is believed to generate a barrier to aid sub-complex turnover, and in an attempt to study the disassembly, enzymatic activity of GDH was suppressed. We recently found that depleted GDH remains in an inactive state and that this state can be recovered by an inclusion of GDN1. To confirm a link between GDH disassembly and the generation of a barrier to efficient turnover of GDH, we differentiated GDH in vivo by whole-cell dissociation and preserved this state. We also investigated the effect of reconstitution of GDH on the disassembly of the other seven enzymes and determined that activity of TPI is favored by reconstitution of GDH in vivo. Moreover, we report that reconstitution of glycolytic enzymes supports an active sub-complex of enzymes, triose phosphate isomerase, TPI, and PDH. This study indicates that GDN1 is sufficient to maintain the glycolytic enzyme assembly state, TPI, by the remaining five glycolytic enzymes.

Statement of significanceHarnessing redox balance has been exploited to develop anticancer and anti-inflammatory agents that target redox mechanisms. Our study confirms that vesicular transport of complexes to the surface of the cell is maintained by GDH and investigates the consequences of disrupting this mechanism. We show that complete disassembly of the glycolytic enzymes, including triose phosphate isomerase, destroys the glycolytic enzyme assembly state, and the implication of resting TPI. Glycolytic enzyme reconstitution may be a strategy to minimize cell injury.

Human mitochondrial transplantation has the potential to cure rare diseases due to deficient function of patients 'soma-encoded' proteins. Likewise, optimizing mitochondrial function can support health span and longevity. However, most existing mitochondria are derived from patients with mitochondrial disease, which hinders their use in clinical contexts. Here, we investigate potential therapeutics through an integrative genomics and machine learning (ML) approach. We trained ML models (that are tailored to collect data from mitochondrial content analysis, proteomics, and transcriptomics) on 600 patient-derived mitochondria. We evaluated the models ability to predict mitochondrial function and health span in six mammalian species using two measurement methods for mitochondrial health span: i) the amount of energy extracted from the mitochondria used and ii) the strain-speci-fic respiration rate per mitochondrion of the total energy delivered. Additionally, we conducted a series of simulations based on a published long-lived plant mitochondrial donor cell experiment. Results indicate that human mitochondrial contents were predicted correctly in all six species, including evidence for variants specific to the species (see Supplementary Section). These results suggest that a machine learning-derived mtDNA database may be the first step toward restoring mitochondrial health and optimizing health span, particularly for plant species.

Peroxisomes are dimeric membraneless organelles that mediate an oxidative, endo- and exochronic degradative cycle. The first turnover of DHA and the second, fatty acid synthesis cycle from DHA requires specific cycles of fatty acid activation, catabolism and synthesis. Enzymatic inactivation by superoxide (O2-) requires oxidative stress and for this reason, mitochondrial and peroxisomal antioxidants (PatN in peroxisomes and RHO in mitochondria) are frequently expressed as byproducts of antioxidant DNA-damage responses. In healthy mitochondria RHO expression is mostly regulated by the proapoptotic transcription factor, BH3-only proteins. But how oxidative stress, once induced by peroxide/superoxide reactions, and extracellular signals evoke the expression of RHO and nuclear receptors from BH3-only genes remain poorly understood. These new data shed light on the critical roles of BH3-only protein RHO and mitochondrial antioxidants, collectively, in the environment induced 'snap' response to oxidative stress.

One Sentence SummaryROS driven peroxisomal damage activates RHO, Rabs, PatN and significantly transforms the peroxisomes and mitochondria.

Key PointsO_LIRHO and the nuclear hormone receptor osterix (OXR) are usually only expressed in mitochondria and are thus considered mitochondrial antioxidants. Under oxidative stress these transcription factors signal for activation of peroxisomal and nuclear cycles.
C_LIO_LIBy the oxidative environment activated mito-patn are transiently activated to a par-level cytoplasmic accumulation and nuclear expression of RHO and osterix, these nuclear receptors are then activated after reversible transcriptional-induced epigenetic changes.

The eccentric mitochondria located on the inner mitochondrial membrane constitute a distinctive but environmentally permissive organelle that regulates cellular fitness, cell cycle and survival. To gain mechanistic insight into these roles, we have created an in vitro system of eccentric mitochondria with human breast cancer cell line MDA-MB-468 cells and used a stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy imaging technique to identify core constructs of the mitochondrial population. We co-culture the cells with varying ratios of several biochemical modulators, which was preceded by labeling of mitochondrion targets. These mixtures recapitulate most of the known effector roles of mitochondria on cells. Our system allowed us to identify the presence and distribution of the canonical messenger RNA mitochondrial target initiation factors, coupled to the classical notion of dysfunctional mitochondria (DMTs) at centers of the cells. We identified higher miR2954 levels associated with core transcriptomic features of mitochondria. Moreover, 2954 reduces miR26a and miR223 levels with phosphorylation at the Ser262 (cytosine-phosphate-choline) by up to 2000-fold, thereby promoting the assembly of ACC27, a mitochondrial determinant, core construct of mitochondria found on the inner and outer membranes. Decreasing ACC27 inhibited core transcriptomic features of the altered condition, thereby confirming an energy conservation strategy. Furthermore, miR26a inhibitors inhibited cell death of MDA-MB-468 cells, in contrast to wild-type cells, which showed growth inhibition by miR26a treatment. These findings were further supported by observing these same messenger RNAs in wild-type and their miR26a - treated conditions, and we confirmed that miR223 knockdown results in cell death and increased apoptosis. Thus, these genetic and biochemical experiments show the regulatory roles of miR26a, miR223 and ACC27 on the cell and the induction of apoptosis by ACC27 knockdown.

Many human tissues and their respective normal populations are housed within a highly protected microenvironment from environmental stress, enhancing their resistance to oxidative and inflammatory insults. Exposure to both oxidative and inflammatory stress both stimulates and prevents the expression of mitochondrial stress resistance markers (MRs) such as ATP6A1 and mitochondrial Unbiased Fermentable Pyruvate Dehydrogenase (UCP1), and primes the cellular mitochondrial morphology to enhance the protection. Here we show that acute and chronic excessive oxidative stress (<6 mmol/L) in 256 healthy human individuals exposed to the presence of nearly ubiquitously expressed MRNA known as LIN21 (MicroRNA Non-Coding Transports 21) are associated with increased circulating UCP1 levels in all tissues and only in men. UCP1 over-expression is strongly associated with reduced 3,3',5,5'-Tetramethylthiuram disulfide (TMTDS)-induced UCP1 levels and H2O2 levels, highlighting the protective nature of UCP1 and TMTDS exposure. A direct association between UCP1 and TMTDS-resistant hepatocyte genotypes was also revealed, whereby UCP1 patients exhibited a more vulnerable phenotype compared to liver fibrotic patients carrying a mutated TMTDS receptor allele. Finally, a high-throughput genome-wide analysis revealed a central role of the H3K36me3 histone lysine tail in the normal recruitment of the UCP1 binding protein 19 (UCP1B19), revealing the existence of a distinct UCP1 promoter by analyzing the GCN5 combinatorial signature in both the genome-wide and UCP1B19 histones levels. UCP1B19 over-expression is also associated with higher oxidative stress response and altered metabolic pathways, emphasizing the role of H3K36me3 in UCP1 regulation. Together, these results uncover the functional associations between non-coding H3K36me3 modifications, mitochondrial stress markers (MRs) and resilience to reactive oxygen/nitrogen stress.

The transcription of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is essential for energy homeostasis and has gained significant research interest. In mitochondria, inhibition of AMPK by pharmacological and genetic methods contributes to cellular senescence, insulin resistance, and cardiac hypertrophy. However, the mechanisms of AMPK inhibition in mammalian cells and its biological significance are not fully understood. With the help of a human stem cell-based model of cardiac senescence, and genetic and pharmacological methods of AMPK inhibition, we provide a comprehensive picture of AMPK activity in living cells, its regulation, and the underlying differences between mouse and human metabolic pathways. We establish that both glycolytic and oxidative metabolism are efficient limits of AMPK activity. The activation of glycolysis and oxidative metabolism leads to rapid expansion of reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels in healthy cells. This, in turn, triggers a decline in AMPK activity in mammalian cells, which is involved in cellular senescence and heart failure. Importantly, AMPK loss-of-function in cardiomyocytes as a function of age does not coincide with the age-related rise in ROS levels, and instead is associated with senescence-induced release of reactive oxygen species. Furthermore, we propose a possible mechanism by which AMPK activation promotes ROS production and prevents ageing.

The malignant transformation of immortalized skin fibroblasts can be accelerated by aldehydes and other low-molecular weight, chemical pollutants, which can trigger cellular reprogramming and inflammatory processes. This process may involve glycolysis and increased mitochondrial activity. Here, we investigate the functions of complex IV to the light chain of the mitochondrial respiratory chain in the formation of stromal transformation. While heme containing complexes have been shown to engage in different reactions in different cell types, no heme containing subcomplex IV complex has been identified in mitochondria before. Our findings confirm that the P3 and P2.2 complexes of complex IV interact with each other to mediate proton exchange reactions.

Sleep deprivation alters the physiological functions of intracellular compartments and nuclear proteins related to circadian rhythms. Mammalian models lack a deep circadian system, making quantifying the effects of sleep deprivation on nuclear proteins in invertebrate models essential. In this study, we assessed the alteration of the expression of nuclear proteins involved in mitochondrial oxidation in the post-sleep state in the Drosophila melanogaster nuclear sphere under the geomagnetic variation using dark imaging and light (mimic of sunset). We found the accumulation of the mitochondrial inner membrane subunit Mfn1a1a (2-oxoglutarate-mannosyl-presistor) following illumination and thus in response to the change in geomagnetic signals. We identified this nucleoid-localized (NUR1)87-38, a TATA-box binding protein for circadian key gene, involved in de novo mitochondrial Mfn1a1a accumulation during sleep under the geomagnetic variation. Finally, we show that NUR187-38 preserves the transcriptional response to the geomagnetic change and regulates circadian transcriptional activity. Together, our findings reveal the molecular basis of the circadian signaling pathway through NUR187-38/mitochondria/TATA-box.

In this second of three papers, we examine red blood cell (RBC) morphometry and RBC-membrane proteomics from our laboratory mouse strain (C57BL/6Case). In paper #1, using stopped-flow absorbance spectroscopy to ascertain the rate constant for oxyhemoglobin (HbO2) deoxygenation (kHbO2), we find substantial kHbO2 reductions with (1) membrane-protein inhibitors p-chloromercuribenzenesulfonate (pCMBS) or 4,4-diisothiocyanatostilbene-2,2-disulfonate (DIDS); (2) knockouts of aquaporin-1 (AQP1-KO), or Rhesus blood-group-associated A-glycoprotein (RhAG-KO), or double knockouts (dKO); or (3) inhibitor+dKO. In paper #3, reaction-diffusion mathematical modeling/simulations reveal that kHbO2 could fall secondary to slowed intracellular O2/HbO2/Hb diffusion. Here in paper #2, blood smears as well as still/video images and imaging flow cytometry (IFC) of living RBCs show that [~]97.5% to [~]98.6% of control (not drug-treated) cells are biconcave disks (BCDs) across all genotypes. Pretreatment with pCMBS raises non-BCD abundance to [~]8.7% for WT and [~]5.7% for dKO; for DIDS pretreatment, the figures are [~]41% and [~]21%, respectively. Modeling (paper #3) accommodates for these shape changes. Light-scattering flow cytometry shows no significant difference in RBC size or shape among genotypes. IFC reveals minor differences among genotypes in RBC major diameter (OMajor), which (along with mean corpuscular volume, paper #1) yields RBC thickness for simulations in paper #3. Label-free liquid chromatography/tandem mass spectrometry (LC/MS/MS) proteomic analyses of RBC plasma-membrane ghosts confirm the deletion of proteins targeted by our knockouts, and rule out changes in the 100 proteins of greatest inferred abundance. Thus, genetically induced changes in kHbO2 must reflect altered abundance of AQP1 and /or the Rh complex.

Mitochondria play a central role in cellular energy metabolism and homeostasis, and their dysfunction is closely linked to the progression of age-related diseases. The mitochondrial ubiquitin ligase MITOL (also known as MARCHF5) is a key regulator of mitochondrial dynamics and function, and reduced MITOL expression in the mouse heart has been implicated in mitochondrial dysfunction and cardiac aging. In this study, we identified berberrubine as a compound that promotes MITOL expression and activates mitochondria. We further assembled a group of berberrubine-based compounds, including its quinoid form and a newly developed water-soluble derivative, and collectively named them "Mitorubin" as mitochondria-activating compounds with therapeutic potential. While conventional berberrubine has poor water solubility, the addition of acetic acid significantly improved its solubility, enabling formulation as a solution. Mitorubin enhanced MITOL expression in cultured cells, increased mitochondrial DNA content and expression of mitochondrial proteins, and promoted mitochondrial respiration. In a model of age-related cardiac dysfunction, oral administration of Mitorubin restored mitochondrial function, improved cardiac performance, suppressed myocardial hypertrophy, and alleviated pulmonary congestion. Moreover, Mitorubin did not shorten lifespan in aged mice and significantly extended lifespan in high-fat diet-fed mice, suggesting both safety and efficacy under chronic administration. These findings suggest that Mitorubin is a promising mitochondrial activator and may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for age-related diseases.

Mitochondrial structural and functional changes accompany psoriasis; however, the mitochondrial response to psoriatic inflammation in keratinocytes and fibroblasts has not been studied. Here, we investigate the effect of psoriasis-like inflammation (PLI) induced by cytokine cocktail (IL-17, IL-22, TNF-) on mitochondrial network morphology and function in living cultured keratinocytes (HaCaT) and fibroblasts (BJ-5ta). In both skin cell types, PLI triggered expression of psoriasis-related SKALP/Elafin and high amounts of cytokines (IL-1, IL-6), interferons (IFN-, IFN-{beta}, IFN-{gamma}), and chemokines (CCL5, CXCL8), accompanied by mitochondrial ROS production, network fragmentation, swelling, and cristae disassembly. STED nanoscopy revealed that the mitochondrial cristae are disappearing in response to PLI, with the process starting faster and being more pronounced in keratinocytes than in fibroblasts. Moreover, in keratinocytes, PLI leads to mitochondrial respiration suppression and elimination of the organelles. These findings of cell-specific mitochondrial responses may guide future investigations into new pharmacological targets for managing psoriasis.

Whether and how podocytes depend on mitochondria across their long post-mitotic lifespan is yet unclear. With limited cell numbers and broad kidney distribution, isolation of podocyte mitochondria typically requires first isolating podocytes themselves. Disassociation of podocytes from their basement membrane, however, recapitulates an injured state that may stress mitochondria. To address this, we crossed floxed hemagglutinin (HA) -mitochondria tagged (MITO-Tag) mice with those expressing Cre in either podocytes (NPHS2) or distal tubule and collecting duct (CDH16), thus allowing for rapid, kidney cell-specific, isolation of mitochondria via immunoprecipitation. Mitochondrial respiration in fresh isolates from young (4-7 mo) and aged (22-26 mo) mice of both sexes demonstrated several previously unreported significant differences between podocyte and tubule mitochondria. First, although podocytes contain fewer mitochondria than do tubule cells, mitochondria isolated from podocytes averaged twice the respiratory capacity of tubule mitochondria when normalized to mitochondrial content by citrate synthase (CS) levels. Second, age-related decline in respiration was detected only in podocyte mitochondria and only in aged male mice. Finally, disassociating podocytes for cell culture initiates functional decline in mitochondria as those from cultured primary podocytes have half the respiratory capacity, but twice the hydrogen peroxide production of podocyte mitochondria isolated directly from fresh kidneys. Thus, podocytes maintain sexually dimorphic mitochondria with greater oxidative phosphorylation capacity than mitochondria-dependent tubules per organelle. Previous studies may not have detected these differences due to reliance on podocyte cell culture conditions, which results in artifactual suppression of mitochondrial function.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is characterized by chronic injury and oxidative stress leading to progressive lung tissue destruction. Emerging evidence suggests that regulated cell death pathways, particularly ferroptosis, contribute to COPD pathology. We previously identified the stress response protein and known ferroptosis inhibitor nuclear protein 1 (NUPR1) as markedly downregulated in lung tissue from COPD patients. Here, we demonstrate that NUPR1 inhibition exacerbates iron accumulation, enhances lipid peroxidation, impairs mitochondrial function, disrupts cellular metabolism, and increases oxidative stress in lung epithelial cells. Furthermore, Nupr1 knockout mice exhibit mitochondrial abnormalities, increased oxidative damage, and lung tissue changes consistent with COPD pathology. Collectively, our findings establish NUPR1 as a critical regulator of ferroptosis, stress responses, mitochondrial integrity, and metabolic balance in the lung, highlighting its potential contribution to COPD pathogenesis.

The incidence of post-cardiac arrest myocardial dysfunction (PAMD) is high, and there is currently no effective treatment available. This study aims to investigate the protective effects of exogenous mitochondrial transplantation. Exogenous mitochondrial transplantation can enhance myocardial function and improve the survival rate. Mechanistic studies suggest that mitochondrial transplantation can limit impairment in mitochondrial morphology, augment the activity of mitochondrial complexes II and IV, and raise ATP level. As well, mitochondrial therapy ameliorated oxidative stress imbalance, reduced myocardial injury, and thus improved PAMD after cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR).

Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) catalyzes the sixth step of glycolysis. As a moonlighting protein, GAPDH interacts with other molecules, seemingly unrelated to glycolysis, to exert additional functions, such as inducing apoptosis. However, specific mechanisms underlying these interactions remain unclear. Therefore, in this study, we aimed to elucidate these mechanisms by analyzing human and porcine GAPDHs based on their three-dimensional (3D) structures using various biophysical techniques, including nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, gel filtration chromatography, and thermal shift assay. Although GAPDH became unstable when nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) was removed (apo state), the 3D structure of the tetramer was maintained regardless of the temperature. However, in the presence of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), GAPDH split into dimers at low temperatures, exposing the interface between the dimers and increasing the flexibility of the side chains at the site. Moreover, subunit splitting also occurred upon exposure to oxidizing agents, such as hydrogen peroxide. These findings suggest that GAPDH maintains a stable tetramer in the presence of NAD+ but becomes unstable and easily oxidized upon NAD+ depletion. When multiple residues, including those other than the cysteine residue at the active site, are oxidized by reactive oxygen species or nitric oxide, or when it interacts with ATP, GAPDH splits into dimers. This subunit splitting may trigger interactions with other molecules.

Mitochondria generate ATP by establishing a proton gradient across the inner membrane, which also drives calcium uptake via the mitochondrial calcium uniporter (MCU), while sodium-dependent NCLX (encoded by SLC8B1) facilitates efflux. The absence of severe phenotypes in MCU-knockout models suggests redundant calcium transport mechanisms. We investigated the role of TMBIM5, a potential bidirectional mitochondrial calcium transporter, by generating zebrafish lacking Tmbim5, Slc8b1, or both. tmbim5-knockout fish exhibited growth impairment, muscle atrophy (particularly in slow-twitch fibers), increased brain cell death, and reduced mitochondrial membrane potential without altering steady-state mitochondrial calcium levels. slc8b1-deficient fish demonstrated significantly attenuated sodium-dependent calcium efflux and increased larval mortality but were otherwise normal. Surprisingly, tmbim5/mcu and tmbim5/slc8b1 double knockouts were viable with normal Mendelian distribution. tmbim5/slc8b1 double knockouts displayed impaired mitochondrial calcium uptake capacity, diminished calcium efflux, and severely disrupted cristae architecture not observed in single knockouts. These findings suggest that Tmbim5 functions predominantly in mitochondrial calcium efflux rather than influx and indicate that robust compensatory mechanisms maintain mitochondrial calcium homeostasis despite disruption of these transport pathways.

Subcellular mitochondrial positioning in cells is necessary for localized energy and signaling requirements. Mitochondria are strategically trafficked throughout the cytoplasm via the actin cytoskeleton, microtubule motor proteins, and adaptor proteins. Miro1, an outer mitochondrial membrane adaptor protein, is necessary for attachment of mitochondria to microtubule motor proteins for trafficking. Previous work showed when Miro1 is deleted (Miro1-/-) from mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), the mitochondria become sequestered to the perinuclear space, disrupting subcellular energy and reactive oxygen species gradients. Here, we show that Miro1-/- MEFs grow slower compared to Miro1+/+ and Miro1-/- MEFs stably re-expressing the Myc-Miro1 plasmid. Miro1-/- MEFs have a have a cell cycle defect with decreased percentage of cells in G1 and increased cells in the S phase of the cell cycle. We conducted the first ever RNA sequencing experiment dependent upon Miro1 expression and found differential expression in cell proliferation and migration genes upon deletion of Miro1, including the MAP Kinase signaling pathway. We find that ERK1/2 phosphorylation is elevated both spatially (cytoplasm and nucleus) and temporally following serum stimulation in Miro1-/- MEFs. We investigated the expression levels and oxidation of the Dual Specificity Phosphatases (DUSP1-6), ERK1/2 target phosphatases. We found no differences in DUSP1-6 expression and oxidation under asynchronous and synchronized cells. Lastly, we evaluated the oxidation status of ERK1/2 and found an increase in ERK1/2 oxidation in the Miro1-/- MEFs compared to Miro1+/+ and Myc-Miro1. These data highlight transcriptional control based off Miro1 expression and demonstrate the highly dynamic regulation of ERK1/2 upon deletion of Miro1 that may support the observed cell cycle and proliferation defects.

Mitochondria, often referred to the powerhouse of the cell, are essential for cellular energy production, and their dysfunction can profoundly affect various organs. Transplantation of healthy mitochondria can restore the bioenergetics in diseased cells and address multiple conditions, but more potentials of this approach remain unclear. In this study, I demonstrated that the source of transplanted mitochondria is not limited by species, as exhibit no significant responses to mitochondria derived from different germlines. Moreover, I identified that metabolic compatibility between the recipient and exogenous mitochondria as a crucial factor in mitochondrial transplantation, which confers unique metabolic properties to recipient cells, enabling them to combat diseases. Additionally, my findings indicated competitive interactions among mitochondria with varying functions, with more bioenergetic-active mitochondria yielded superior therapeutic benefits. Notably, no upper limit for the bio-enhancement provided by exogenous mitochondria has been identified. Based on these insights, I proposes a novel therapeutic approach--adaptive bio-enhancement through mitochondrial transplantation.

sample_q_texts: The brain relies on the hierarchical organization of afferent signals to maintain functional coordination. This organization likely operates on multiple time scales, with distinct signals operating on longer versus shorter timescales. To examine how neural activity reflects different signaling channels, we analyzed EEG from two frontoparietal networks of interest: early sensorimotor and later parietal and prefrontal areas. We identified time series of spiking activity as a powerful driver of information in the sensorimotor network, based on the number of modulating connections. We validated this framework using two EEG datasets from five human subjects in the near- and far-frontoparietal networks. In both datasets, subjects performed a simple task - performing various response-contouring finger flexion and extension movements to a target object. We find distinct features for the spiking signal and exploit this heterogeneity in response time to examine response-contouring behavior across sensorimotor layers. First, we show that both spiking and response-contouring activity were highly correlated at early sensorimotor layers and only weakly correlated at later layers, aligned with the functional architecture of the sensorimotor network. Second, we find that time scales of response-contouring responses and sensorimotor spiking activity are distinctly distinct, with shorter response-contouring responses operating at longer timescales than sensorimotor spiking. In the far-sensorimotor network, subjects first reported localizable, high amplitude, responsiveness responses. These are strongly correlated with short time scales in sensorimotor spiking activity, and weaker with longer time scales. These findings may represent a striking underestimation of information flowing through the sensorimotor network given the presence of shorter time scale responses in the spiking activity. In the more medial, or posterior, area of the frontoparietal network, subjects report peaks of localizable, high amplitude responsiveness responses, with activity mostly oriented along the long axis of the brain. These responses are strongly correlated with longer time scales in response-contouring activation, but weakly correlated with sensorimotor spiking responses in response-contouring amplitudes. Thus, while a potential driver of network information may be the short timescale of response-contouring activity, in sensorimotor areas further back from the visual cortex, responses are oriented along the long axis of the brain.

We extract affordances from sensory experience to predict the extent of embedded information and optimize perceptual decisions. Dissociations in the associative sensorimotor system have the potential to support this sensory-to-action mapping. Here, we examined this possibility using computational models of the human sensorimotor cortex, where activation patterns were predicted from perceived sensory input using sensory-to-action predictions generated from intracranial recordings of healthy human participants. Contrary to prior assumptions, the data did not reveal the presence of redundant modular distributed representations in sensorsimotor representations. Instead, the results showed that while hierarchical structure may emerge during training, individual members of modular clusters specialized in areas and shared a distinct set of functional connections between neurons and clusters during generalization training. This independent specialization allowed for robust sampling from the sensory-to-action prediction across divergent output streams. Our findings demonstrate that functional specialization of cortical sensory-motor representations is not sufficient to support the propagation of affordances. Instead, hierarchical structure arises due to mechanistic tuning that customizes sensory-motor mappings for specific input configurations.

Atypical spatiotemporal fluctuations of neural population activity have been observed during task-related behaviors in human functional neuroimaging. One possibility is that patterns of population activity, such as attractors, are induced under certain processing constraints and may affect behavior. We examine relationships between deviations from deterministic attractors, described by Lyapunov exponents and lower-extremum projections, and early cortical processes in active reach-to-grasp (RTG) and object-holding (OH) movements. While deviations from deterministic attractors following external disturbances were found in all rhythms (including those associated with movements), internal dynamics indicated absence of deterministic attractors, with few deviations and a lack of stability in OH and RGT. Behavior simulations with these attractors generated with diminishing RGS-O activity (reduced connections with the periphery) suggested that such attractors are formed within the presynaptic layer. This finding has implications for the temporal control of cursor location and hand motions in human RTGs.

Significance StatementBiological rhythms in human behavior have been used to understand and control brain activity, although rhythmologists typically consider this a passive influence. Rather than passively receiving subcortical regulation from cortex, this study emphasizes a proactive role for active control by cortex on rhythm production. The information in the neural control system, also defined by Lyapunov exponents, allows active, cortical-dependent control over these rhythms.

Using PET, we demonstrate that motor imagery enhances only areas rich in motor cortical projections and those that commonly mediate motor execution. Specifically, spinoparietal cortex and premotor cortex are more active under the influence of mmi. We provide an exploratory and comprehensive causal analysis of the delayed effect of mmi on limb movement despite only 20 minutes of training time (~2h per day). In line with this, and consistent with the other effects of mmi, the difference in motor performance between the motor task and mmi phase differs greatly during training time. In addition, no difference emerges between the motor task phase and the mmi phase for any frontal brain region or resting state. Consistent with previous findings, mmi enhances the production of dynamic brain responses, particularly lower temporal resolution responses, in areas contributing to motor learning and related primary motor circuits. Our study shows how mmi enhances the organization of brain activity during a motor task and outlines additional specific effects of mmi on brain activity, including by influencing dynamic responses.

The planning stage of motor control initiation is crucial for the timely execution of skilled movements. In the right (r) and left (l) hemisphere, planning is primarily dependent on synergies between cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic circuits, yet their neural relationship remains debated. In this study, we investigated the effects of a bimanent stimulation of the left and right cerebral hemispheres on premotor cortex motor planning during movement execution. We recorded neural signals from 32 motor-trained participants during the motor sequence facing left and right. These participants received bilateral stimulation within 10 min before their movement to bilateral or unilateral control conditions. Using multivariate pattern analysis, we quantified synergistic and antagonistic associations across left and right hemispheres. Specifically, we measured the largest single-neuron effects in left motor cortex for the control left sequences, while the largest group of synergistic interactions occurred between left and right frontal and cingulo-opercular cortex in the control right sequences. Regional antagonistic interactions were characterized by the greatest decreases at the levels of the central thalamic nuclei and thalamo-cortical connections, which are related to the initiation of movement, as evidenced by reduction of motor power in the subjects. Our results provide new insights into the neural modulation of motor sequencing in the right and left hemispheres. This study has identified novel neuroanatomical mechanisms of multisensory and unilateral integration in sensorimotor sequencing.

C_LIO_LIThis increases the number of contacts in the motor cortico-thalamo-cortical regions, which is known to increase the heterogeneity of sensorimotor sequencing
