The ability to predict the progression of voluntary movements relies on the temporal integration of neural and motor representations. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), we investigate how auditory vision-motion interactions contribute to the neuronal dynamics underlying the initiation of performing movements under various conditions. First, using fMRI data collected from individuals with and without optic ataxia (OA), we demonstrate that isolated FA patients demonstrate comparable neural activation patterns to controls. Second, auditory vision-motion interactions exhibited differential 90-degree and 180-degree neural encoding in both groups, suggesting an interaction with the timing of motor action. We further show that the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) is engaged with information about the spatial position of the impending movement in both groups, and provide evidence that the mPFC supports the neural timing and spatial encoding of motor movements with strong interaction effects across OA. Finally, demonstrating that mPFC is involved in the integration of aomotor-sensory information in both groups, we present an explanation for the discrepancy of auditory vision-motion interactions between the groups regarding the timing of motor execution.

Strategies to improve movement initiation from the central nervous system are fundamental to human movement, yet the underlying brain mechanisms remain poorly understood. While previous work has suggested that specific brain regions, the dorsomedial thalamic nucleus (DMt), have a key role in motor initiation, they have largely been analyzed in particular motor behaviors. Here, we evaluate whether motor commands are part of the functional organization of the motor thalamic nucleus (MTx). We used intracranial electrophysiological recordings from 18 healthy adults to decode movement directions from somatosensory activity (motor thalamic discharge) while they performed two familiar movements that recruited distinct but task-relevant regions of the cortico-striatal-motor network: a right-handed slice of the counterclockwise circle maneuver and a right-handed grip of a water bottle. We observed robust motor responses of the DmtL (samarang) in both behaviors. DmtL firing correlated with different movement patterns and was associated with sensory-motor intentionality and reward-based control, but not with mirror movement or response time. Together, these findings suggest that DmtL is necessary for motor command encoding but plays different roles in different movements.

A key challenge in neuroscience is understanding how information is transformed in the brain. Sensory signals are frequently transformed in the brain into internal representations, which can then be used to generate motor actions. An intriguing hypothesis contends that perceptual features and their interactions within sensory areas, rather than sensory data, are transformed into representational representations that activate distinct motor areas, allowing for the identification of target objects. However, measuring sensory representations is challenging and requires the use of highly invasive procedures that may compromise the participants welfare and induce behavioral resistance. Here we report a neuromonitoring procedure that enables the monitoring of sensory processes throughout a stimulus sequence within healthy participants. Furthermore, it utilizes relatively low-cost and non-invasive EEG. We examined the activation of an occipital area in response to sparse stimuli in visual cortical areas V1 and V2. We found that responses in both regions appeared in sequence and in response to the stimulus sequence. This putative signature of sensorial processing could be coupled to better detect attentional control or further investigated in tasks where anticipation plays a crucial role.

Contextual affordances that figure in a complex variety of brain dynamics underlying perception and cognition play key roles in shaping visual experience, mental imagery, and experience, while a plethora of neuroimaging studies has exposed how they transform neural dynamics governing ones embodiment in neural networks. Despite early reports on the existence of such associations, a causal relation between embodied imagery and brain activity has so far remained an open issue. In this study, we investigated the relation between mind-brain-body activity and the trajectory of the perceived stimulus in a single subject across two contrasting settings, with task-unrelated continuous 2D surfaces and dynamic scenes-of-change stimuli. We obtained concurrent functional magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography (fMRI-EEG) data from one healthy adult. The results showed that the topological information encoded in the scene-of-change stimulus in the higher visual regions elicited activation in a nonlinear spontaneous EEG network with predominant theta (4-8 Hz) dynamics and a local partial spiking network with high alpha (>20 Hz) dynamics. This nonlinear electrophysiological signature of scene-of-change stimuli was also evident in the fMRI datasets, though with a marginally larger contribution to basal ganglia-thalamus network-associated results during vision than to the behavioral task. During wakefulness, brain activity involving postural muscles became associated with gaze-guided lighting of the scenes-of-change stimuli during the task. In conclusion, our findings suggest that neural activity-dependent embodied schemas are registered by distributed cortical and cerebellar dynamics which mediate cognitive decision-making, visual perception, shaping sense of embodiment in neural networks, and behavioral functioning.

To adapt to sensory perturbations, the brain rapidly co-opts previously learned processing strategies from diverse sensorimotor cortices. While several regions show high-frequency co-activation in sensory adaptive tasks, how and when learned reorganization occurs across the cortical hierarchy remains unclear. To investigate how different cortical populations co-activate during adaptive processing, we recorded multimodal neural dynamics in sensorimotor cortical areas and circuits while monkeys actively engaged in the Cat Trap maneuver. Using multi-scale analysis, we identified bi-directional parallel spiking co-activation in primary sensorimotor cortices and mediodorsal thalamus at single-point time scales. Then, we performed a functional network approach to identify the top-ranked cortical clusters most strongly connected to adaptive behaviors: primary sensorimotor cortex, somatomotor premotor cortex, and thalamic RTI1-VLPVC regions all co-activated in a pattern consistent with a cascade of planned, target-guided cortical reorganization. This includes executive, attention, and sensorimotor control regions that increase while task-related and subserve adaptive behavior. These results reveal a progressive reorganization of sensorimotor cortical networks over time, highlighting central coordination between diverse cortical populations.
sample_p_texts: The brain coordinates multiple parallel motor programs, ensuring synergy and preventing interference during movements. Yet, performance often degrades when brain-machine interfaces are used during concurrent tasks or ongoing movements. We suggest that latent neural representations may represent a strategy to solve this issue. In this study, we addressed this question using neural signals from a tetraplegic individual with partial residual motor function, implanted with a wireless epidural electrocorticography (ECoG) device. By adapting dimensionality reduction techniques, we found that motor execution and motor imagery span partially overlapping subspaces in mesoscale neural signals, shaped by specific frequency band contributions. Despite substantial shared variance, we show that identifying orthogonal, condition-specific dimensions enables successful decoding of executed and imagined movements, even when performed simultaneously. These findings show that ECoG signals can expose separable neural subspaces, allowing executed and imagined actions to be harnessed independently and in concert. This opens a promising avenue to develop brain-machine interfaces that can simultaneously control multiple external devices or operate alongside natural movements.

Movement planning processes must account for body posture to accurately convert sensory signals into movement plans. While movement plans can be computed relative to the world (extrinsic), intrinsic muscle commands tuned for current limb posture are ultimately needed to execute spatially accurate movements. The whole-brain topology and dynamics of this process are largely unknown. Here, we use high spatiotemporal resolution magnetoencephalography (MEG) in humans combined with a Pro-/Anti-wrist pointing task with 2 opposing forearm postures to investigate this question. First, we computed cortical source activity in 16 previously identified bilateral cortical areas (Alikhanian, et al., Frontiers in Neuroscience 2013). We then contrasted oscillatory activity related to opposing wrist postures to find posture coding and test when and where extrinsic and intrinsic motor codes occurred. We found a distinct pair of overlapping networks coding for posture (predominantly in {gamma} band) vs. posture-specific movement plans ( and {beta}). Some areas (e.g., pIPS) only showed extrinsic motor coding, and others (e.g., AG) only showed intrinsic coding, but the majority showed both types of codes. In the latter case, intrinsic codes appeared slightly before extrinsic codes and persisted in parallel across different cortical areas. These findings are consistent with two cortical networks for 1) direct feed-forward sensorimotor transformations to intrinsic muscle coordinates (for rapid control) and 2) computations of extrinsic spatial coordinates, possibly for use in higher-level aspects of visually-guided action, such as spatial updating and internal performance monitoring.

Significance statement / author summaryIt is thought that the brain incorporates posture into extrinsic spatial codes to compute intrinsic (muscle-centered) motor commands, but the whole-brain temporal dynamics of this process is unknown. Here we employed human magneto-encephalography (MEG) to track this process across 16 bilateral cortical sites. We identified two, largely overlapping subnetworks for posture-dependent intrinsic codes, and extrinsic spatial coding. Surprisingly, the direct transformation from sensorimotor coordinates to intrinsic commands preceded the appearance of extrinsic codes, suggesting that extrinsic motor codes are derived from intrinsic codes for higher-level cognitive purposes.

The coordination of forelimb and orofacial movements to compose an ethological reach-to-consume behavior likely involves neural communication across brain regions. Leveraging wide-field imaging and photo-inhibition to survey across the cortex, we identified a cortical network and a high-order motor area (MOs-c), which coordinate action progression in a mouse reach-and-withdraw-to-drink (RWD) behavior. Electrophysiology and photo-inhibition across multiple projection neuron types within the MOs-c revealed differential contributions of pyramidal tract and corticothalamic (CTMOs) output channels to action progression and hand-mouth coordination. Notably, CTMOs display sustained firing throughout RWD sequence and selectively enhance RWD-relevant activity in postsynaptic thalamus neurons, which also contribute to action coordination. CTMOs receive converging monosynaptic inputs from forelimb and orofacial sensorimotor areas and are reciprocally connected to thalamic neurons, which project back to the cortical network. Therefore, motor cortex corticothalamic channel may selectively amplify the thalamic integration of cortical and subcortical sensorimotor streams to coordinate a skilled motor sequence.

Multisensory integration constitutes a fundamental neural mechanism essential for understanding complex cognitive processes and variations inherent in neuropsychiatric and neurological conditions. Although multiple theoretical models exist to account for the computational processes underpinning this mechanism, there is an absence of a consolidated framework that facilitates the examination of multisensory integration across diverse experimental and computational contexts. We introduce Scikit-NeuroMSI, an accessible Python-based open-source framework designed to streamline the implementation and evaluation of neuro-computational models of multisensory integration. The utility of the framework is shown by modeling spatiotemporal causal inference at various analytical levels using Bayesian and network models of multisensory integration, addressing a critical research question of the field. We also offer recommendations for the enhancement of this software and propose directions for future research using this integrative methodology.

sample_q_texts: Cadherin molecules promote homoeomerism of planar tissues, allowing precise planar and planar-hinge animal tissues to generate in plants (heteromerization) and eyes (quadrinomers) in animals. To understand the evolutionary and developmental routes of cadherin homoeomerization, we tracked evagination stages in mutants that lack prior cellular events needed for budding (pf-clen and scll-e2), heteromerization (pcll-e2), and quadrinomer formation (fz-el and pb-el). Analyses revealed a nascent cadherin complex appears in the exosome compartment of buds where developmentally processed cadherins and glycogen are exocytosed. Transgene overexpression of cadherin protein results in upright and 3-dimensionally elongated cadherin-cadherin complexes that appear at the point of budding, heteromerization, and quadrinomer formation. These complexes are made and secreted from the endosomes of cortical secretory vesicles in addition to the newly formed exocytic vesicles (exocytosis-evagination); this provides a mechanism to both render extracellular binding sites proteinogenic and to orchestrate complex shedding from the cortical endosomes. The transcriptional response to cadherin upregulation varied between mutants with two different cadherin proteins but mostly involved early steps in cadherin-cadherin homoeomerization, heteromerization, and quadrinomer formation. We suggest this is likely a metabolic regulation that may be conserved across deuterostomes and has been evolved in all animal phyla and animalia.

Amphipod and copepod larvae possess cilia, specialized micro-organelles evolved to sweep over food particles and to transport essential nutrients to the gastro-intestinal tract. The mechanobiology of cilia generation, though crucial for the successful colonization of physical media such as sand and mud, is poorly understood. Using biophysical modeling and simulations, we present a high-resolution investigation of the regulation of larval cilium morphogenesis, a topic currently limited to simple models of tadpole-like species. We show that emergence of the larval cilia from the sino-motile unit requires a tripartite coordination of four evolutionarily distinct genes responsible for performing different functional aspects of cilia biogenesis. Our analysis resolves the role of a dual splicing locus and offers evidence of a prior redundant establishment of two alternative splicing patterns with contradictory splicing outcomes. Such a pattern of editing transcripts has been observed in stem-cell-like, planarian gastrulation, and in recent research on mammalian somatic tissues, suggesting a possibly general underlying requirement for a coordinated upstream step of precision editing. The biological relevance of our findings is supported by insights on the evolution of enzymatic mechanism involved in streamlining the cilium production during larval development.

Morphogenesis is a complex process that involves sequential cellular events. To investigate cellular trajectories within environments of complexity, we developed a time-resolved imaging approach, Timelapse, in developmental biology using the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans. Timelapse provides long-term imaging of cell-specific processes from single cells to single organisms in vivo. Timelapse is based on rotation-tracking microscopy coupled with software written in the Python framework matplotlib. Timelapse can distinguish between cell morphologies, indicates rapid accumulation and differentiation of different cell types in planarians, facilitates observation of several spatial aspects of cilia from individual C. elegans cells, and provides overall improved performance over conventional methods when used on complex developmental systems. Timelapse can be used to interrogate early processes such as prediction of position of cell types and organization of cilia with resolutions much better than those achieved by conventional fluorescent imaging techniques. Timelapse can also be used to study cell-specific developmental trajectories in complex environments such as the head and posterior of the planarian C. elegans. Timelapse is a general purpose software for fast, easy, and high-throughput time-lapse imaging of individual organisms. The Timelapse website has examples of working scripts and demos.

Planar cell polarity formation is a fundamental property of animal development, and perturbation of this process causes various developmental defects. Detailed measurements of polarized patterning require the availability of advanced imaging instrumentation. Here, we describe a firmware stack enabling the manual integration of GigE support into Acquire (BX5.3/C2.2) on the Axio-Focus Inquire (MF3-200D8T) or the Axio-Focus Z1 (MF4.5) on the Swiss-IX bench. This stack is documented using worms, Caenorhabditis elegans, fruit flies, zebrafish, and alligators, along with plant apical meristem patterning experiments. The stack enables accurate, continuous fixation and tissue cross-sectioning with GigE inspection and complete pair-tracking tracking, with full handling by user manual at the bench. This work supports the preparation of new colonies and provides an aid to continue the investigation of biological problems affecting polarity regulation.

In the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, sterile colony formation is mediated by the pinocytic sensor Perc, forming astellular progeny sacs whose viability is considered an adaptive response to UV stress and other environmental disturbances. Perc signaling has been linked to several cellular processes, including activation of the cyclin-dependent kinase C-Raf kinase, which ultimately facilitates flagellar growth and division. In this study, we investigated the involvement of Perc in flagellar shape. We demonstrate that genetic disruption of the Perc gene alters the structure of the embryo flagellum in an apically-biased manner. Circular plasmids expressing Mus musculus Curt1, which drive the Gremlin-activating protein, Kurtdc1, perturb peripheral and apical flagellar morphology via Curtdc1 subcellular interactions. The loss of the Curtdc1 nuclear localization motif triggers transcriptional response which involves modulation of MdmA, a crucial epigenetic regulator of genome stability. Consistent with this, Curtdc1 disruption triggers the melting of genome-wide chromatin marks, which is increased following Curtdc1 loss-of-function mutations in cytoarchitecture of somatoplasm. Both Curtdc1 disruptions cause colonic segregation of stem cells. Furthermore, we observe a reduction in cilia in two Curtdc1 deletion strains, while Perc alterations do not affect cilia maturation status. Taken together, our results indicate that Perc signals contribute to the overall shape of an apically biased flagellar that enables division of astellular progeny sacs. These results suggest that astellular progeny size is modulated by interaction of the discriminative sensory pathway with nuclear signals and stability control systems.

Epiboly, the apical expansion of the blastoderm groove during blastula morphogenesis in Caenorhabditis elegans, initiates rapid cell differentiation that generates germ layers, cell types, and tissues. To elucidate the molecular mechanisms of epiboly initiation in C. elegans, we analyzed the mosaic expression of a set of genes that are co-localized with epiboly regulators (DREB1, DREB2A, DNX17, GNRH1) in various blastomeres. This in situ analysis uncovered a gap between both sets of cell division and epiboly onset, which coincided with the end of an entire cell cycle. We identified a prior requirement for DTR10 to initiate epiboly in embryonic stem cells, inducing expansion of the basolateral limb at the end of G2 and its arrest at the G1/S transition. We then investigated the transcription factors responsible for initiating epiboly, identifying two additional genes (DREB18, GEL1) as DTR10-dependent epiboly drivers that initiate cell division and epiboly simultaneously at two rounds of cell division, without a complete gap between them. We also found that DTR10 itself activates DREB1, another gene with potential epiboly functions, and identified a set of DTR10-binding DNA motifs that promote its transcriptional activation. Finally, we show that DNX17 binds to DNA within the epiboly zone and activates GNRH1 expression, thereby regulating epiboly initiation. Our results reveal a distinct transcriptional regulation that spans both cell cycles during mitosis and epiboly initiation, and indicate the importance of the nuclear atpase complexes in mediating Ep2-ep1 localization by modulating DTR10-associated epigenetic chromatin dynamics.

Golgi apparatus are unique to eukaryotes and organelle function and motility is highly conserved across the six major lineages. The development of the Golgi is still poorly understood and its diversification is not yet a topic of widespread research. Here, we use cryosectioning and cryo-electron microscopy to analyze the microstructure of wild-type C. elegans salivary gland and its variants to quantify the distribution and production of endoplasmic reticulum components of the Golgi. We show that the Golgi of the Lcdmt4 mutant is frequently morphologically abnormal and that the Golgi morphology resembles the Drosophila Mnph and Dsg2. Additionally, we show that the Lcdmt4-Golgi is a weak importer of dsm2, which drives the transition from a typically lipid-rich to actin-rich state. Despite the resemblance to the Drosophila Golgi, we observed that some Golgi diffusion-related vacuolar proteins differ between the two mitoxytonuclear genomes, both being abundant in the Drosophila muscle tissues. These findings suggest that this organism possess a unique Golgi apparatus that is still evolving and being adapted to the fly life-style.

Cell junctions play a pivotal role in maintaining tissue integrity and host-specific functions, yet a comprehensive view of their formation has remained elusive. Here, we present a comprehensive 3D atlas of Drosophila cilium-like structures (dCesMUS), spanning the entire appendage length, and demonstrate how their architecture changes across species and cell types. We analyzed cell-type and cell-to-cell connectivity, cellular sizes, and assembly on a single cilium. Leveraging published cell marker data, we identify both somatic and stem cell-derived dCesMUS. Over 3.5 billion cells, 3.5 billion dCesMUS are identified across the larval and adult tails, totalling 11.3 billion dCesMUS, by combining clonal cell populations with single cilium delineation. Our analyses are complemented by a comprehensive 3D reconstruction of each cilium structure and established global cell connectivity. Compared to pseudopods, dCesMUS are more exposed to cellular and chemical stimuli, dynamically adapt their functional roles, and display larger sizes. Together, these findings provide a unified framework for dissecting the Drosophila ciliogenesis process and show how cell identity may underlie cilium structure and function.

Single-nucleus transcriptome studies present significant opportunities to map cell state in multiple tissues, unraveling the molecular features underpinning diseases and revealing pathways that regulate differentiation. The hallmark of somatic embryo cells is nuclear karyotyping, a process where the nuclei of a large subset of cells with identical diploidy are ordered one by one with no overlap, thus creating two distinct clones. If multiple nuclei from a single cell are retained during karyotyping, it may contain an extra copy of the haploid chromosome and be called a chimera nucleus. Chimera nuclei have been detected in hundreds of cell types but have remained challenging to distinguish between due to their high mutability and propensity to undergo frequent cell division. Here we present Ciliogeneticome (CiliO) a next-generation genome-resolved workflow for karyotyping, which reduces stochastic cell death and spatial cloning of chimera nuclei. Application of CiliO for genome-resolved karyotyping in C. elegans and zebrafish revealed 66 chimeran nuclei across tissues across species including astrocytes, cranial ganglia, dorsal nerve cord, and ventral nerve cord. Analysis revealed that: while two chimera nuclei carry identical diploidy, others bear a single ancestral nucleus or a variant chromosome; chimera nuclei are enriched in pluripotent precursors and somatic cells; thus, chimeran nuclei that are present in developmental stages of precursor cells are less likely to survive karyotyping; and more chimera nuclei are located at the boundaries of tissues than centres. Our approach facilitates comprehensive study of chimeran nuclei and transforms cell type-specific and spatial analysis for cell states in multi-modal scRNAseq studies.

Understanding the molecular and cellular dynamics of invertebrate cell division is critical for unraveling the mechanisms behind species-specific cell behaviors. Alpinuleid isopods, such as the stick insect (Hemiptera), are among the longest-lived arthropods on Earth and exhibit uniquely modified cell division, known as the extruded shaft cell cycle. However, the mechanisms underlying their unique cell divisions remain poorly understood. Here we performed genome-wide transcriptome analysis of cohesin-associated DvoF (cdvF) gene transcripts during the active developmental phase of stick insect cells. To highlight novel transcriptional events at cell divisions, the in silico analysis identified two highly conserved cell cycle phases and four cell division-specific gene expressions of the cohesin complexes during cell division. Notably, we observed a rapid upregulation of cohesin proteins during meiosis phase 2, while the upregulation of cohesin components starts earlier at the germination phase. We also revealed the complex intracellular dynamics of cohesin proteins during meiosis and germination phases. Altogether, the analysis of cohesin components during cell cycle phases offers insights into cell division dynamics, survival, and non-typical developmental time in insect cells.
sample_p_texts: The bilaterian through gut with an anal opening is a key invention in animals, since it facilitates effective food processing, which allows animals to grow to a larger body size. However, because non-bilaterian animals lack a through gut, the evolution of anus is still debated. The formation of bilaterian hindgut is governed by the spatial expression of several transcription factors (e.g. Caudal and Brachyury) under the control of Wnt signaling. This conserved pattern has been used to support the homology of the anus of protostomes (insects, snails) and deuterostomes (sea urchins, humans). Here we show, that these bilaterian "hindgut" marker genes are expressed around the male gonopore of several xenacoelomorphs, which have a blind gut without an anal opening. These findings suggest a deep evolutionary relationship between the xenacoelomorph male gonopore and the bilaterian anus. Since xenacoelomorphs are the potential sister group to all remaining Bilateria, our results suggest that the bilaterian anus evolved from a male gonopore that came in contact with the digestive endoderm to form the posterior opening.

The cyst of the protist ciliate Vorticella efficiently differentiates into teletroch, the free-swimming stage. Here, using video microscopy and quantitative imaging we establish that the cyst differentiation follows two strict temporal and spatial patterns. The temporal pattern is initially marked by the functional formation of the contractile vacuole, which then discharges its fluid into the neoformed cytopharynx and, in a third stage, into a membrane invagination which, to the rhythm of the vacuole, differentiates into an oral cavity exhibiting a polarized cilia array revealed by -tubulin immunostaining. Two poles delineate the spatial pattern. The apical pole is defined by the position of the pre-existing papilla, which determines the site of oral cavity formation directly below it. The second basal pole is placed at the rupture point of the cyst wall. It is characterized by {beta}-actin accumulation and allowed release of the telotroph according to its basal-apical polarity. Both the temporal and spatial patterns are impaired by concanamycin A treatment, a specific inhibitor of vacuolar type H+-ATPases altering functions of contractile vacuoles. The findings indicate that cyst to telotroch transition is predetermined by the location of the papilla on the cyst wall and under the control of a functional contractile vacuole. We propose that Vorticella cyst is a simple single-cell model for investigating basic principles of integrative neogenesis of organelles in Protozoa, and of apical-basal cell polarity in Eukaryotes.

Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) germ granules are hallmarks of germ cells across the animal kingdom and are thought to be hubs for post-transcriptional regulation that promote formation of the germ cell precursors. While numerous RNAs are associated with germ granules in Drosophila, the functions of many in germline development are poorly understood. Current methods for RNA knockdown, such as RNAi, do not allow local depletion of transcripts such as those found in the germ granules. We leveraged CRISPR-Cas13 to create a subcellular RNA knockdown system and tested it on two mRNAs, nanos (nos) and sarah (sra), whose abundance in germ granules differs. Because Cas13 has both cis and trans cleavage activities, we evaluated the effect of target abundance on off-target RNA depletion. We show on and off-target RNA depletion is coupled when targeting the more abundant nos germ granule transcripts. Off-target RNA knockdown is less potent when the system is used for less abundant sra transcripts. When sra is knocked down in germ granules, we observe defective primordial germ cell migration, and an increase in the calcium indicator GCaMP at the posterior, consistent with sra encoding a negative regulator of calcium signaling. In sum, we report an in vivo Cas13-based system for subcellular knockdown, evaluate its feasibility, and uncover a novel function for sra germ granule transcripts in promoting germline development.

Progenitor cell dedifferentiation is important for stem cell maintenance during tissue repair and age-related stem cell decline. Here, we use Drosophila ovarian germ cells as a model to study the role of cytonemes in BMP signalling-directed dedifferentiation to germline stem cells. We provide evidence that differentiating germ cell cysts extend cytonemes towards the niche during dedifferentiation to reactivate BMP signalling. We show that the Enabled (Ena) actin polymerase is localised to the tips of germ cell cytonemes and is necessary for robust cytoneme formation, as its mislocalisation reduces the frequency, length and directionality of cytonemes. Furthermore, specifically perturbing cytoneme function through Ena mislocalisation reduces germ cell BMP responsiveness and the ability of differentiating cysts to dedifferentiate. We discuss how cytonemes may be widely used by differentiating cells to re-establish niche contact and signal responsiveness following stem cell loss, promoting robust dedifferentiation of stem cells in diverse contexts.

Cell polarization and cytokinesis are fundamental processes in organismal development. In the Caenorhabditis elegans model system, both processes are partially driven by a local inhibition of contractility at the cell poles. Polarization is triggered by centrosome-directed, local inhibition of cortical contractility at what becomes the posterior pole, while cytokinesis occurs when spindle elongation-dependent astral relaxation combines with centralspindlin-induced accumulation of myosin at the cell equator. During both processes, Aurora A (AIR-1) kinase is activated on centrosomes and diffuses to the cortex where it inhibits the guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) ECT-2, attenuating RHO-1 activation and actomyosin-based contractility. While these biochemical processes have been characterized experimentally, a quantitative understanding of how this circuit drives cortical dynamics in polarization and cytokinesis is still lacking. Here, we construct a mathematical model to test whether a minimal set of well characterized, essential elements are necessary and sufficient to explain the spatiotemporal dynamics of AIR-1, ECT-2, and myosin during polarization and cytokinesis of C. elegans. We show that robust establishment of polarity can be obtained in response to a weak AIR-1 signal, and demonstrate the relevance of rapid ECT-2 exchange and a persistent AIR-1 cue during polarization. In the minimal model, the rapid turnover of ECT-2 causes a quasi-steady response to changes in the AIR-1 signal, and transient asymmetries are not self-sustaining. After tuning the model for polarization, we demonstrate that it can accurately predict ECT-2 accumulation during cytokinesis, suggesting a quantitative similarity between the two processes.

Intraflagellar transport (IFT) coordinates the transport of cargo in cilia and is essential for ciliary function. CILK1 has been identified as a key regulator of IFT. The mechanism by which it acts has, however, remained unclear. In this study, we use fluorescence imaging and single-molecule tracking in the phasmid cilia of live C. elegans to study the effect of the CILK1 homolog DYF-5 on the dynamics of the IFT. We show that in the absence of DYF-5, IFT components accumulate at the ciliary tip. kinesin-II is no longer restricted to the proximal segment of the cilium but is present all throughout the cilium, while its velocity is different from that of OSM-3. The frequency of IFT trains is reduced and in particular retrograde trains were rarely observed. In the absence of DYF-5, retrograde transport is vastly reduced, resulting in the accumulation of IFT components at the tip and depletion at the base. The latter results in impeded anterograde train assembly, resulting in fewer trains with irregular composition. Our results show that DYF-5 plays a key role in regulating the turnarounds of IFT trains at the ciliary tip.

Complex eukaryotes generally experience some degree of ecological transition as they develop, which is usually accompanied by the expression of different traits across their ontogeny. Theory suggests the evolution of differentiation between life stages is facilitated by the expression of different genes at different points throughout ontogeny, which alleviates pleiotropic evolutionary constraints. Therefore, ascertaining what contributes to specialized patterns of gene expression across ontogeny is fundamental to understanding the evolution of ontogenetic complexity. Expression divergence between duplicate genes and gene organization on chromosomes have been identified as important features of relatively complex ontogenies. Therefore, one could predict that their link to transcriptional specialization across ontogeny may be weaker in relatively simpler life cycles. Here, we investigated the links between gene duplication, gene organization, and stage-specific patterns of expression across the relatively simple Caenorhabditis elegans life cycle. We found that signatures of stage-biased chromosomal regions were weaker in C. elegans than what has been previously described in organisms with more complex ontogenies. Furthermore, we found the extent that duplicate genes varied in ontogenetic expression pattern was more constrained in C. elegans. Overall, our findings add to a body of evidence that suggests a link between gene duplication and gene organization and the evolution of complex ontogenies.

Intercellular bridges are essential to connect developing germline cells. The Drosophila melanogaster egg chamber is a powerful model system to study germline intercellular bridges, or ring canals (RCs). RCs connect the developing oocyte to supporting nurse cells, and defects in their stability or growth lead to infertility. Despite their importance, it has been technically difficult to use electron microscopy-based approaches to monitor changes in RC structure during oogenesis. Here, we describe the application of a complementary set of volume EM-based approaches to visualize ultrastructural changes in the germline RCs. The combination of array tomography (AT) and focused ion beam (FIB) scanning electron microscopy (SEM) has allowed us to gain insight into previously unappreciated aspects of RC structure. We were able to quantify differences in RC size and thickness within and between germ cell clusters at different developmental stages. Within a cluster, RC size correlates with lineage; the largest RCs were formed during the first division, and the smallest RCs were formed during the fourth mitotic division. We observed the formation of membrane interdigitations in the vicinity of RCs much earlier than previously reported, and reconstruction of a RC from a mid-stage EC provided insight into the 3D orientation of these extensive cell-cell contacts. Our imaging also revealed a novel membrane structure that appeared to line the interior of the RC lumen. Although the focus was on ultrastructural changes in the germline RCs, our dataset contains valuable details of additional cell types and structures, including the fusome, the germline stem cells and their niche, and the migrating border cells. This imaging framework could be applied to other tissues or samples that face similar technical challenges, where the small structure of interest is located within a large sample volume.

The Drosophila intestine is a powerful model for stem cell dynamics and epithelial biology, yet no intestinal derived cell lines have been available until now. Here, we describe the establishment of Drosophila intestinal cell lines. The cell lines were derived from the embryonic intestine through specific RasV12 expression and show continuous proliferation and the ability to be frozen and re-thawed. Each derived cell line exhibited morphological and cellular heterogeneity. Single-cell RNA sequencing confirmed their intestinal origin and cell populations with unique enriched signaling pathways. In addition, L15, one of the three lines, formed 3D spheroids that displayed epithelial polarity. Together, these lines provide an additional resource for studying intestinal development, epithelial organization, and pest management.

In developing epithelia, cells become planar polarised with asymmetric localisation of the core planar polarity proteins to opposite cell membranes, where they form stable intercellular complexes. Current models differ regarding the signalling mechanisms required for core protein polarisation. Here, we investigate the existence of cell-intrinsic cell-scale signalling in vivo in the Drosophila pupal wing. We use conditional and restrictive expression tools to spatiotemporally manipulate core protein activity, combined with quantitative measurement of core protein distribution, polarity and stability. Our results provide evidence for a robust cell-scale signal, while arguing against mechanisms that depend on depletion of a limited pool of a core protein or polarised transport of core proteins on microtubules. Furthermore, we show that polarity propagation across a tissue is hard, highlighting the strong intrinsic capacity of individual cells to establish and maintain planar polarity.

sample_q_texts: The epithalamus contains hundreds of giant neurons that are assumed to be sensory processors. Some these and similar structures are located in the brain's lateral ventricle (LV) while others surround it, forming so-called interectopic chambers (IECs). The neural activity in the laminae of IECs is supposed to be a correlate of the processing of incoming afferent impulses received by the sensory neurons located there. This has been tested by providing IECs of different volume and number with afferents. Different afferent stimulus patterns were compared in IECs of different volume and number, and in both light and auditory afferents. The transmission of signal via higher-order neurons was hypothesized to differ between the two patterns. In the older literature, the concept of higher-order neurons was rather vague and no direct measurements were available. However, in the last years, measurable average thresholds of simple signal patterns have been obtained. For example, below a threshold, a chimpanzee model neuron located in the IECs was assumed to be noiseless. Previous simulations predicted the shapes of IECs: a lower number of IECs means a higher volume, larger IECs and/or larger hemispheres. The models found could thus be applied for all possible values. We found a difference in the signal generation by afferents of different origin between models with different number of IECs, and in all models the signal originated mainly from afferents of the lateral and anterior auditory areas, independent of the number of IECs. However, in every model, the signal originating from the dorsal cochlea was the largest and similar to the signal originating from the medial and lateral temporal areas, corresponding to the areas most activated in these areas. This result, however, cannot be interpreted in terms of stimulus interpretation, based on sensory areas lateral and anterior to the IECs. We suggest that this difference must also have other causes than the ones known from the previous literature.

BackgroundThe cerebellum is thought to regulate a diverse set of behaviours relevant to survival, yet existing cerebellar function modeling relies on incompatible models that disregard the large body of evidence that support a localization of cerebellar input regulation to cortical areas. In particular, cerebellum-targeted models routinely give primacy to dendritic connectivity parameters of mossy fiber inputs and have neglected spiking connectivity in cortex, as well as the performance of cerebellar networks under single fiber input conditions.

MethodsIn this multi-scale, synthetic modeling study, we use population spike rate and spikeset data from patients receiving functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) tracking of cerebellar activity to reproduce spike rate as function of time and of cerebellar spiking populations (d1 spiking curves) across cortical and cerebellar networks. We then integrate this reproduced spiking curves into mechanistic cerebellar dynamics (d2 models) using a biophysically motivated model of multisynaptic cerebellar dynamics. Finally, we tune model parameters using model parameters validated against published patient datasets to account for observed relationships between edema score and cerebellar spiking curves (a neurological binary score used to assess cerebellar damage).

FindingsAll models that replicate the average hippocampal subfield (BCP-2) data (total spike rate, d1 spiking curves, and mean d2 spiking curve) show an increase in total spike rate with both aging and edema. When we replicate the individualized hippocampal subfield (BCP-1) data with spike rate invariance (spiking subpopulations are equally weighted), edema scores lead to a larger increase in total spike rate (d2 model), while younger animals have a larger decrease (d2 model). Taken together, this demonstrates that while there is little to no decrease in total spiking rate with age, the increase in spiking subpopulations may be substantially greater than the decrease in cortical spiking subpopulations in older rats (with estimates being  5-fold and  25-fold respectively). Finally, we demonstrate that edema score strongly correlates with expected changes in d2 activity and provides a neurological binary binary assessment of cerebellar damage.

Interpretation: this study highlights the importance of replacing the current mossy fiber-centric dominant model of cerebellar spiking with a mechanistic cerebellum-cortical network model. Centralized to adult cerebellum, these dynamical models will provide insight into the strength and underlying mechanisms supporting cerebellar performance benefits in the cortical network.

In animals, two distinct neuronal circuits emerge soon after birth during the formation of the cerebral cortex in early development. Understanding their neuronal maturation depends on the spatial and temporal analysis of our fast-varying neocortex.

Here, we investigated two interlinked questions in parallel: what is the amplitude of the light-evoked response in neocortex in early development (the stable rod-like contribution after high-intensity visual stimulation)? How does the amplitude change in different developmental epochs?

We performed both electrophysiological analyses with a locally optimized electrostimulation system of a fluorescent calcium indicator and a high-resolution axial imaging of unoxygenated 3T 16V MRI equipment, where we could quantify the neuronal response in the laminar distribution of both the dorsal and the ventral visual areas. We observed strong amplitudes of the visual evoked response, with highest amplitudes being emitted from the central vision and decreasing towards the visual cortex. The amplitude decreased in different regions with maturation. Specifically, the dorsal and the ventral visual areas, show peaks in early development, showing a diminished amplitude in mid-adolescence. After the age of 8, the strength of the evoked response is approximately at 50%.

In summary, we show that the first synaptically-gate-controlled three-neuron circuit responsible for vision forms in the cortex already at birth, while the second circuit requires maturation to manifest its strength. The dendrite-neuron circuit activity is weaker for stimuli of higher complexity as the child approaches maturity. Our results, to our knowledge, are the first to comprehensively reveal changes in the amplitude and timing of the variable light-evoked response across developmental stages in this spatially- and temporally-restricted region of the mammalian brain.

The neocortex is the largest and most complex brain region, representing about one-third of adult human brains mass. Due to the large polar orientation field of neocortical neurons, it is highly susceptible to bidirectional communication between neighboring regions. Therefore, sensory signals as well as the physiological state of the organism often have close influence on the functional activity of a neighboring cortex. Given this, neuronal activity of a sensorimotor area, crucial for everyday tasks such as motor learning and behavior, should be closely related to that of a neighboring cortex. The relationship between sensorimotor and covert cortical areas relies on the complexity of networks which contain both depolarizing and hyperpolarizing (anodic/cathodic) sub-networks. Anodic/cathodic gradients are associated with many psychological disorders, such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, where abnormal activity in anodic/cathodic gradients has been observed in clinical subjects, supporting its application as a marker for the spectrum of neuropsychological conditions. However, the relationship between pathological anodic/cathodic gradients and cortical networks, which have been largely studied individually, remains unclear. Here, we analyzed network properties of neurons of select anodic/cathodic gradients in a set of nondepressed adult brain hemispheres of genetically related mouse models of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. We mapped anodic/cathodic gradient properties onto the anodic/cathodic gradient in the GO neural network. We found a linear relationship of network properties of anodic/cathodic gradients with the application of anodic/cathodic gradients to the GO neural network for a wide range of gradients. Finally, we found evidence of network dependence on anodic/cathodic gradients for a subset of gradients. This study provides evidence for an axis-aligned relationship between pathological anodic/cathodic gradients and cortical network structure, whose application to dBlock-based network reconstructions across cortical connectivity can provide novel insights into pathological conditions, e.g., the increase in network complexity due to abnormalities in anodic/cathodic gradients has been implicated in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

Neuronal signals are carried by the action potentials (AP) that are rapidly transmitted along axons. However, the dynamics of individual APs is not well understood. The latest optical microscopy technique, in situ functional serial image averaging (SI-FIA), can follow the action potentials that travel along axons in living brain tissues. However, the speed of the AP is limited. In the case of optical fiber probing, the number of pulses per millisecond is up to 30 or even 90 for most techniques. Optical imaging techniques have reached short-duration, high-frequency action potentials. Here, we further increase the speed of follow-up methods and demonstrate a 4-photon second order OCO detection technique that reaches sub-millisecond action potentials. With 36 optical pulses per second, the technique can follow individual APs at 180 hertz for 10-second acquisition time. We then analyzed the results. We have demonstrated the ability to detect and label APs and oligomeric assemblies within a short-lived molecular complex such as the cyclic di-GMP-binding protein (cd-GMP) family and lactosylceramide biosynthesis complexes (LACs). This suggests that the kinetics of both individual APs and oligomeric complexes can be studied using the 4-photon OCO technique.

A major goal of neuroscience is gaining a deep understanding of the brains biological basis of cognition and behaviour. For some years, automated tools have become important tools to facilitate certain brain-related experimentation. A further area of application has been the description of brain state of awake animals using electrophysiology techniques such as EEG, EMG and EEG-EMG. The quantification of these states is of the utmost importance for understanding both human and animal behaviour and brain function. Nevertheless, current tools, or even software options, for the quantification of these brain states often remain limited, especially regarding their applicability. In particular, quantification and comparing of brain state maps generated by different tools presents challenges since different stimuli and physiological measurements are known to affect the overall map. In addition, there is a high user dependency and it can be very difficult to translate between tools to generate a similar map from one tool to the next. We describe a method that combines the analysis of 2D recordings from experiments on awake 2-cell and 3-cell neurons in a mouse brain tissue, a.o. the RRIM experiment. The method consists of adjusting the image reconstruction parameters in order to optimise the reconstruction of the EEG-EMG activity of each 2- or 3-neuron group and at the same time account for the combination of stimuli used in each experiment. We demonstrate the potential of our method for the generation of reliable brain state maps.

Author summaryThe brain can be thought of as its own living organism and the machinery required to maintain its function must be found in its neural network structure. Within this structure, dendrites and other cell bodies are likely to be involved in the monitoring and regulation of the nerves signals within the network. Mapping of brain-related signals, e.g. neural activity, is challenging since different types of measurements affect how signals are recorded. This all affects the extracted brain state maps and researchers may find it difficult to interpret the maps to the same degree. In this work, we show that their use in research protocols is challenging, even when the same type of stimulation methods are used. We therefore introduce a new method for generating working brain state maps that are well similar between different experiments and experiment times.

Learning a motor action often involves simultaneous control of their actions and attention. Recently, the theory of serial habituation (SH) has emerged as a unifying framework explaining how spatial attention modulates action, in particular, by guiding the projection of articulatory movements in the space. However, its inference has been limited by the lack of high-resolution neuronavigated visual stimulation recordings of specific subpopulations of the motor cortex with accurate synaptic temporal resolution. Here, we develop a high-resolution visual stimulation paradigm in which the motor cortex is reliably labelled and visualized via high-resolution in-vivo synaptic tracer, enabling their accurate observation in real time. By recording the theta-burst power (3-5 Hz) of a methylblue-labeled calcium imaging fibre photometry in three motor cortex regions, we demonstrate how specific spatial attention depends on presynaptic response in the parvalbumin (PV) interneuron, whose nuclear responses reflect the pyramidal neuron firing thresholds. This corresponds with earlier putative SH-mechanism in the LCSTM of the caudal subthalamic nucleus (LSTN). The inhibition of pyramidal neuron activity by PVs by converging heat shock proteins (HSP70) reduced the theta-burst power of LSTN axon terminals while the theta-burst power increased with pyramidal neuron hyperactivity. This SH rhythm corresponded with pyramidal neuron activity that modulated presynaptic-transient synaptic strength and the presynaptic pool size. Taken together, we present a new paradigm in which spatial attention to the space modulated presynaptic-transient and presynaptic pool sizes in the caudal subthalamic nucleus of the substantia nigra pars reticulata (LSTN-SNR). This paradigm has significant implications for understanding the brain-behavior connection between action and attention.

The brain integrates sensory information and cognitive processes, such as perception and motor control. However, our understanding of the neural mechanisms that sustain and support sustained activity is limited. Here, we employed the mouse gyroscope (Gyroscope) Drosophila line, a genetically tractable model of cortical auditory processing to investigate the role of auditory post-central cortex 4 (pc4) in sustained activity. We found that phonotopic electrophysiological responses of pc4 depolarize during sustained sound exposure, implying a role in sustained auditory activity. However, functional connectivity analyses suggested that the gp4 local field potential is unable to support sustained activity. Conversely, the spontaneous activity of the ep48-gp4a interneuron network, a functional connectivity hotspot in pc4, demonstrated sustained activity. To identify the basis of sustained activity, we investigated the ablation effects of parvalbumin (PV)-expressing interneurons in the unilinage of the pc4-ep48 network. We identified the c288T/G sequence in the mouse vGluA3-IL2 mRNA to have an increase impact in the ability to maintain sustained activity. Our findings emphasize the significance of local field potentials to support sustained processing in the pc4. The identified c288G sequence in the mGluR5 receptor-containing protein, the mGluR5, likely contributes to the sustained activities of ipGNAP and its subsequent suppression.

It is well established that information of spatial structure can propagate from neuronal subcircuits to excitatory cortical areas with rapid-high, high, and low spiking rates. However, the mechanisms by which neuronal subcircuits organize and transport spatial information to cortical areas are not well understood. Here, we examined the spatiotemporal information propagation dynamics between hypothalamic nucleus of the solitary tract (NST) and hippocampi that are essential for the progression of a long-lasting sleep onset state. We used high-field magnetic induction light-induced tracing in mice to record the single-cell spiking activity. The conditioned activity pattern could be injected at any point in the NST and showed a sequence of rapid-high, high and slow spatial propagation dynamics to the mouse internal auditory cortex (MAC) at 10 Hz. However, slow propagation was observed to the mouse macaque monkey brain at 4-14 h after conditioned bathing injection, where spatial information could be propagated with high speeds at 300-800 ms latency from NST. We speculated that slow-spreading of spatial information from NST to macaque monkey brain during the sleep onset state is caused by spike synchronization between afferent and efferent neurons.

Asters scientists recently demonstrated how particular neuronal population oscillations in the single principal neuron generate astrocyte firing activity in the glomerular cell layer in the sight organ retina. To better understand how astrocytes and their characteristic striated appearance support and perpetuate the asterozoon-like oscillations, we used a state-of-the-art high-density microstructural imaging of awake mice. Astrocytes also stimulated by light pulses within 4 ms to recreate the light-evoked oscillations in the principal neuron activated, when integrated with the corresponding firing activity, entirely recapitulated the in vivo single-cell oscillations in the astrocyte layer. Moreover, the integrated oscillograms of the astrocytes and principal neurons exhibited inter-tissues synchrony, thus confirming that this system can be modeled as a syncytium within a purely neural oscillator. The alternate coupled time-series of the visual cortical fields in the mice were registered with the most brain area in which asterozoon-like oscillations were observed--the retinal principal neurons, firing at a similar level as their entorhinal field peers but with more than 5 times faster oscillation speed, revealing the electrophysiological origins of the synchronous visual cortical fields. In addition to the physiology of these frequencies, a fourth putative molecular factor--the release of glutamate from non-oculo-vesical astrocytic terminals into the ophthalmic venous plexus--seems likely to contribute to these activities.
sample_p_texts: Gamma-frequency oscillations ([~]30-160 Hz) are a hallmark of neuronal syn-chronization, yet the fine-scale temporal arrangement of spikes within individual gamma cycles remains poorly understood. Here, we examine head direction (HD) cells in the mouse anterodorsal thalamic nucleus (ADn)--a circuit distinguished by prominent high-gamma activity--to uncover the principles governing gamma coordination. We reveal two fundamental mechanisms: (i) a stable anatomical gradient in which neurons firing earlier in the gamma cycle exhibit longer anticipatory time intervals (ATIs), and (ii) a dynamic rate-phase shift whereby spike timing advances as the animals head aligns with a neurons preferred direction. Together, these results delineate a spatiotemporally structured framework for gamma synchronization, advancing our understanding of the functional roles and circuit mechanisms underlying gamma rhythms in local brain networks.

Gamma oscillations (25-70 Hz) can be induced in the visual cortex by presenting stimuli like gratings. Large stimuli produce two distinct gamma oscillations in primate primary visual cortex (V1) - slow (25-40 Hz) and fast (40-70 Hz), possibly due to different interneuronal networks. While fast-gamma has been shown to strongly lock spikes, slow-gamma does not, and hence its role in cortical processing is unclear. Here, we studied potential influence of gamma rhythms on neural activity using phase-amplitude coupling (PAC). We recorded spikes, local field potential and electrocorticogram (ECoG) from V1 of two adult female monkeys while presenting stimuli that simultaneously induced both gamma rhythms, and developed a novel method that reduces the influence of spike-related-transient on PAC. Interestingly, while fast-gamma showed coupling with frequencies above 150 Hz, reflecting spike-locking, slow-gamma showed PAC in a distinct frequency range between 80-150 Hz, which was especially prominent in ECoG. PAC varied with orientation and spatial frequency in the same way as power in the respective frequency bands, confirming dissociation in the coupling of the two gamma rhythms. Thus, fast-gamma could be more involved in spike-locking, while slow-gamma could represent a modulatory signal acting by amplitude modulation between 80-150 Hz at a more global scale.

Significance StatementGamma oscillations in the visual cortex can be induced by stimuli like gratings, producing two distinct gamma oscillations: slow (20-40 Hz) and fast (40-70 Hz). While fast-gamma strongly locks spikes, the role of slow gamma is unclear. Oscillations have been proposed to influence processing through phase-amplitude coupling (PAC). We recorded spikes, local field potential (LFP) and electrocorticogram (ECoG) from female monkeys and developed a new method to study PAC. While fast-gamma showed PAC with 150-500 Hz, reflecting spike-locking, we found PAC between slow-gamma and 80-150 Hz, which was especially strong in ECoG. The two PAC signatures varied differently with stimulus, reflecting distinct origins. Thus, while fast-gamma could lock spikes, slow-gamma could modulate amplitudes between 80-150 Hz at a global scale.

During wake, sound-evoked and spontaneous neural activity of the auditory cortex evolve in distinct subspaces whereas anesthesia disrupts sound responses and merges these spaces. To evaluate if similar modifications of the sound representation geometry explain sensory disconnection during sleep, we followed large neural populations of the mouse auditory cortex across slow wave sleep and wakefulness. We observed that sleep dampens sound responses but preserves the geometry of sound representations which remain separate from spontaneous activity. Moreover, response dampening was strongly coordinated across neurons and varied throughout sleep spanning from fully preserved response patterns to population response failures on a fraction of sound presentations. These failures are more common during high spindle-band activity and more rarely observed in wakefulness. Therefore, in sleep, the auditory system preserves sound feature selectivity up to the cortex for detailed acoustic surveillance, but concurrently implements an intermittent gating mechanism leading to local sensory disconnections.

The classification of neuronal types is a complex task with numerous molecular, anatomical, and functional (electrical) features have been identified as informative in discriminating neuronal populations. The functional characterization of neurons has traditionally been carried out with predefined sets of parameters such as firing rate and action potential generation threshold. Here we provide an objective method to choose what parameters are most informative about a neurons functional cell type. Using this method we show that despite the significant molecular and anatomical variability across neurons, functional characterization of neuronal activity identifies 9 and 11 distinct neuronal subpopulations in the upper layers of the somatosensory and visual cortices respectively. This novel classification method will help to unravel the functional (electrophysiological) diversity of cellular classes throughout the nervous system. Further, the thorough comparison between the different classes of cells will provide a solid building block for the study of the sensory cortices.

Odor information is transmitted from the olfactory bulb to several primary olfactory cortical regions in parallel, including the anterior olfactory nucleus (AON) and piriform cortex (Pir). However, the specific roles of the olfactory bulb and cortical outputs in wider interactions with other interconnected regions throughout the brain remain unclear due to the lack of suitable in vivo techniques. Furthermore, emerging associations between olfactory-related dysfunctions and neurological disorders underscore the need for examining olfactory networks at the systems level. Using optogenetics, fMRI, and computational modeling, we interrogated the spatiotemporal properties of brain-wide neural interactions in olfactory networks. We observed distinct downstream recruitment patterns. Specifically, stimulation of excitatory projection neurons in OB predominantly activates primary olfactory network regions, while stimulation of OB afferents in AON and Pir primarily orthodromically activates hippocampal/striatal and limbic networks, respectively. Temporally, repeated OB or AON stimulation diminishes neural activity propagation brain-wide in contrast to Pir stimulation. Dynamic causal modeling analysis reveals a robust inhibitory effect of AON outputs on striatal and limbic network regions. In addition, experiments in aged rat models show decreased brain-wide activation following OB stimulation, particularly in the primary olfactory and limbic networks. Modeling analysis identifies a dysfunctional AON to Pir connection, indicating the impairment of this primary olfactory cortical circuit that disrupts the downstream long-range propagation. Our study for the first time delineates the spatiotemporal properties of olfactory neural activity propagation in brain-wide networks and uncovers the roles of primary olfactory cortical, AON and Pir, outputs in shaping neural interactions at the systems level.

Spiking activity along synaptic circuits linking primary somatosensory (S1) and motor (M1) areas is fundamental for sensorimotor integration in cortex. Circuits along the ascending somatosensory pathway through mouse hand/forelimb S1 and M1 were recently described in detail (Yamawaki et al., 2021). Here, we characterize the peripherally evoked spiking dynamics in these two cortical areas. Brief (5 ms) optogenetic photostimulation of the hand generated short ([~]25 ms) barrages of activity first in S1 (onset latency 15 ms) then M1 (10 ms later). The estimated propagation speed was 20-fold faster from hand to S1 than from S1 to M1. Amplitudes in M1 were strongly attenuated. Responses were typically triphasic, with suppression and rebound following the initial peak. Evoked activity in S1 was biased to middle layers, consistent with thalamocortical connectivity, while that in M1 was biased to upper layers, consistent with corticocortical connectivity. Parvalbumin (PV) inhibitory interneurons were involved in each phase, accounting for three quarters of the initial spikes generated in S1, and their selective photostimulation sufficed to evoke suppression and rebound in both S1 and M1. Partial silencing of S1 by PV activation during hand stimulation reduced the M1 sensory responses. Overall, these results characterize how evoked spiking activity propagates along the hand/forelimb transcortical loop, and illuminate how in vivo cortical dynamics relate to the underlying synaptic circuit organization in this system.

The BraiDyn-BC (Brain Dynamics underlying emergence of Behavioral Change) Database offers an extensive, multimodal dataset that links wide-field calcium imaging of the mouse neocortex to comprehensive behavioral measurements during a behavioral task. As one of the contents in this database, we newly provide a dataset that includes 15 sessions spanning two weeks of motor skill learning, in which 25 mice were trained to pull a lever to obtain water rewards. Simultaneous high-speed videography captures body, facial, and eye movements, and environmental parameters are monitored. The dataset also features resting-state cortical activity and sensory-evoked responses, enhancing its utility for both learning-related and sensory-driven neural dynamics studies. Data are formatted in accordance with the Neurodata Without Borders (NWB) standard, ensuring compatibility with existing analysis tools and adherence to the FAIR principles. This resource enables in-depth investigations into the neural mechanisms underlying behavior and learning. The platform encourages collaborative research, supporting the exploration of rapid within-session learning effects, long-term behavioral adaptations, and neural circuit dynamics.

Tactile representations in the barrel field of the primary somatosensory cortex of rodents (wS1) receive inputs from two distinct thalamic nuclei, the ventro-posterior-medial nucleus (VPM) and the posterior medial complex (POm). Previous work has revealed a sweep-stick code in rat wS1 by using a novel whisker velocity-white noise stimulus. Sticks refer to high velocity single whisker bumps, while sweeps correspond to large multiwhisker displacements with extended temporal profiles. We hypothesized that barrel cortex neurons inherit  stick responses from the VPM and  sweep responses from the POm. Here we test this hypothesis by studying the coding strategy of both thalamic nuclei and wS1 in mice. We found a stratified wS1 representation of both sweep and stick functional classes, whereas VPM and POm contained mainly stick encoding neurons. Cortical layer 4  stick responses are a delayed version from VPM, while layer 5b  sweep responses come from POm. Notably, layer 5a  sweep responses result from a temporal integration of  stick information from VPM and POm. Our results put forward a circuit scheme in which fast encoding stick events from VPM allow a fine-tuned texture processing in the cortex, modulated by sweep-responding cells that integrate multi-whisker information.

A number of cognitive and sensory processes are characterized by strong relationships between the timing of neuronal spiking activity and the phase of ongoing local field potential oscillations. The coupling of neuronal spiking activity in neocortex to the phase of alpha oscillations (8-12 Hz) has been well studied in monkeys but remains largely unexplored in other mammals. How these relationships differ between brain areas and cell types, and how they relate to somatosensory signal detection and decision making, are not well understood. We used high density microelectrode arrays to chronically record neural activity from somatosensory cortex, prefrontal cortex, striatum, and amygdala in mice performing a head-fixed whisker-based selective detection task. We observed strong spontaneous alpha phase modulation of single neuron spiking activity as mice performed the task. The prevalence and strength of alpha phase modulation differed significantly across regions and between cell types. Phase-modulated neurons exhibited greater changes in spiking activity during task execution than their unmodulated counterparts. Furthermore, alpha modulation of neuronal spiking during baseline activity correlated with task performance. In particular, many neurons selectively exhibited strong alpha modulation of spiking activity prior to correct trials, but not prior to incorrect trials. These data suggest that dysregulation of spiking activity with respect to the ongoing alpha oscillation may characterize lapses in task engagement or attention.

Astrocytes, which are increasingly recognized as pivotal constituents of brain circuits governing a wide range of functions, express GABA transporter 3 (Gat3), an astrocyte-specific GABA transporter responsible for maintenance of extra-synaptic GABA levels. Here, we examined the functional role of Gat3 in astrocyte-mediated modulation of neuronal activity and information encoding. First, we developed a multiplexed CRISPR construct applicable for effective genetic ablation of Gat3 in the visual cortex of adult mice. Using in vivo two-photon calcium imaging of visual cortex neurons in Gat3 knockout mice, we observed changes in spontaneous and visually driven single neuronal response properties such as response magnitudes and trial-to-trial variability. Gat3 knockout exerted a pronounced influence on population-level neuronal activity, altering the response dynamics of neuronal populations and impairing their ability to accurately represent stimulus information. These findings demonstrate that Gat3 in astrocytes profoundly shapes the sensory information encoding capacity of neurons and networks within the visual cortex.
